articles.title: At the UN, plans for a global coalition to attack LGBTQ+ and reproductive rights
articles.author: Uncloseted MEdia
paras: Far-right activists are trying to dismantle global protections for LGBTQ+ people under the guise of ‘family values’
Originally published on Global Voices
US President Trump speaking at the U.N. General Assembly. Photo by The White House. Fair use.

This article by Hope Pisoni was originally published by Uncloseted Media, an LGBTQ+ focused investigative news outlet, on October 1, 2026. An edited version is being republished on Global Voices as part of a content partnership agreement. It has been edited for length and style.

On September 17, while the United Nations (U.N.) was hosting its annual General Assembly for diplomats and leaders from all over the world, several key figures filled a room across the street at the Millennium Hilton in Midtown Manhattan. Attendees included Trump administration officials, leaders of anti-LGBTQ+ hate groups, far-right politicians from Latin America and reporters from far-right media.

These people were meeting for the Global Forum for Life, Family and Freedoms, a two-day summit of right-wing leaders with an ambitious goal to create a new “pro-life and pro-family” Core Group at the U.N.

Since 2008, the U.N. has had an LGBTI Core Group with 42 member states whose mission is to advocate for LGBTQ+ rights on a global stage. But the organizers of this new group hope to create an opposing organization to push for policies that undermine reproductive and LGBTQ+ rights around the globe.

Aarón Lara, the Mexico-based conservative activist who came up with the idea for the group, said in an August article that the existing LGBTI Core Group has only been successful because there has not been organized conservative opposition, which a new core group would provide.
Lara (left) speaking with a reporter in the Dominican Republic in March. Screenshot via Central Noticias YouTube.

“[The LGBTI Core Group] has successfully established victimhood narratives and incorporated observances with global impact. … I always use this example: If it were a soccer match and one team failed to show up, the winner by default would be the team that was present,” Lara said.

Lara and other supporters of the group agreed at the forum to draw up plans for its creation in the coming months. They may be encouraged to move quickly because the group’s leaders have said they want to use the U.S.’s global influence and capitalize on the current administration’s anti-LGBTQ and anti-abortion stance to do it. The U.S. recently left the LGBTI Core Group, an early move by Trump in his second term.

The LGBTI Core Group describes itself as “an informal cross-regional group of United Nations Member States.” While it is not an official U.N. body, its work includes ensuring that LGBTQ+ people are considered and protected across all of the U.N.’s activities, from humanitarian aid to human rights resolutions.

For example, one of the first U.N. resolutions to reference LGBTQ+ people was one protecting civilians against extrajudicial executions. When some members tried to remove LGBTQ people from those protections, advocates and allies fought to keep them in place. Maria Sjödin, executive director of Outright International, an NGO that focuses on supporting LGBTQ rights worldwide, told Uncloseted Media that work like this could be in jeopardy should the new core group come to fruition.

“We’re talking about the protection of some very basic human rights, and that the opposition to that is trying to organize to make it even more difficult to pass such a thing is really quite horrible,” she says.

Core groups are not official U.N. bodies, so there is no strictly required procedure for their creation. While there have been other core groups established at the U.N., the LGBTI group is unique in that it is designed for continuous operation on multiple issues rather than as a response to a specific conflict or crisis. The “pro-life, pro-family” core group would change that, threatening to shift the balance of power at the U.N.

Ipas, an international NGO that seeks to increase access to safe abortions and contraception, shared a briefing paper, “The Pro-Life and Pro-Family Core Group: The Evangelical Architecture Supporting Anti-Gender Initiatives at the United Nations,” with Uncloseted Media. It explains that this core group would allow anti-LGBTQ+ and anti-abortion governments to collaborate on “coordinated voting” to “dilute, block, or impose conditions on language regarding sexual and reproductive health and rights.” The briefing also predicts that the core group would accelerate existing efforts to portray anti-LGBTQ+ politics as “sovereign resistance” against “globalism” in the public eye.

“This discourse … asserts national sovereignty over agreed-upon international human rights, reframing sexual and reproductive rights as an external imposition rather than as already recognized human rights standards,” the briefing reads.
The first CIVF, held in Mexico City in 2017. Image from CIVF via Wikimedia Commons. CC BY-SA 4.0.

Lara is the founder and president of the Ibero-American Congress for Life and Family (CIVF). Founded in Mexico City in 2017, CIVF describes itself as “Un movimiento de reforma moral, educativa, social y jurídica por la vida y la familia” (a movement for moral, educational, social, and legal reform for life and family) and is best known for holding an annual congress for leaders, primarily from Latin America and Spain, to discuss the promotion of socially conservative policies.
In a 2021 article in an evangelical publication, Lara said that his group had applied to become a core group at the U.N.
“We have the conviction that it is our responsibility as believers to be a light in the midst of darkness, this is why [we] are making this big effort,” he said.
The third CIVF, held in Panama in 2019. Image from CIVF via Wikimedia Commons. CC BY-SA 4.0.

While that application never came to fruition, Lara remained interested in starting a U.N. core group, and announced in July 2026 that CIVF — which did not respond to Uncloseted Media’s request for comment — was launching a new plan to do so.
How did the US get involved?

The following month, Lara shared more details of the plan with The Washington Stand, a news outlet owned by Family Research Council, a Southern Poverty Law Center-designated anti-LGBTQ hate group closely affiliated with Focus on the Family. In the article, Lara says the goal is for the U.S. to sponsor the new group because of its powerful position on the world stage.

Sjödin is concerned about U.S. involvement in a group like this. “[It] already has an outsized influence on the world, so the U.S. potentially taking on a leadership role in a coalition like this also risks the effects being outsized and makes this an initiative that is going to be more difficult to challenge,” she says.
Valerie Huber speaking at CPAC Hungary in 2022. Image by Elekes Andor via Wikimedia Commons. CC BY-SA 4.0.

To that end, CIVF enlisted Valerie Huber, an influential American ally based in Washington, D.C., in their fight. Huber, who co-led the September 17th forum alongside Lara, is an American right-wing activist who held multiple leadership roles at the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) during Trump’s first term. She has consistently promoted the exclusion of LGBTQ+ people in her work — the organization she led before getting her HHS appointment released a guideline that said “it would be inappropriate and unethical to assert or affirm” trans kids’ genders.

“Valerie Huber is internationally recognized in the anti-rights space,” Wendy Via, co-founder and president of the Global Project Against Hate and Extremism, told Uncloseted Media. “She is bringing some credibility [and] influence to the idea of creating a separate core group, so she’s gonna be able to get people to join with her.”

During her tenure at HHS, Huber helped craft the Geneva Consensus Declaration on Promoting Women’s Health and Strengthening the Family (GCD), an agreement between 46 countries, including the U.S. under both Trump administrations, affirming a commitment to hardline opposition to abortion and promoting the heteronormative nuclear family “as foundational to society.”

Critics have noted that many of the agreement’s signatories are led by notoriously authoritarian governments with harsh restrictions on LGBTQ+ people. For example, Saudi Arabia’s maximum penalty for gay sex is death, and Russia classifies the “international LGBT movement” as an extremist group.

During his first week in office, former president Joe Biden withdrew the U.S. from the GCD just months after its launch, stating, “It is the policy of my Administration to support women’s and girls’ sexual and reproductive health and rights in the United States, as well as globally.”

But Huber, now out of her government job and leading the anti-abortion NGO Institute for Women’s Health (IWH), continued to champion the agreement. She’s traveled around the world meeting heads of state, including in Burundi and Argentina, who would quickly go on to join the GCD, while developing more concrete plans to carry out its goals. IWH did not respond to a request for comment.

Within the first week of Trump’s second term, the U.S. rejoined the agreement, and in June, the U.S. assumed the leading secretariat position among its signatories. Via says pushing the core group initiative while the U.S. is the secretariat is likely strategic timing.

“The U.N. is seen as the boogeyman for far-right and Christian Nationalist groups, because their definition of human rights is expansive and inclusive, which is not what these organizations want,” Via says. “But they’re gonna work within the system because it looks like they have an opportunity.”
Huber has advocated in favor of the core group since August and has said that the GCD is “the substantive basis” for the work ahead.

“What has not yet been built is the intentional, sustained coordination that turns a shared commitment into shared strategy at the international negotiating table,” she told The Washington Stand. “A nation that arrives at a negotiation alone is outmatched. A nation that arrives having strategized with 40 others is not.”
The who’s who of the far right are on board
Faith leaders praying over Donald Trump in March 2025. Image via The White House. Fair use.

The September 17th forum was held in the hopes of creating a roadmap to execute the plans for the core group. The event was sponsored by Well Versed, an evangelical NGO whose mission is to bring “biblical principles of governance to government leaders and the people who elect them.”

The forum attracted a number of noteworthy guests. There were three representatives from the Trump administration, including Deputy Secretary of State Christopher Landau, Director of HHS Global Affairs Bethany Kozma, and Ellie Cohanim, the senior policy advisor at the U.S. mission to the U.N.

Leaders from several U.S.-based right-wing organizations also made appearances, including Turning Point USA Faith, C-Fam — which holds special consultative status at the U.N. — and Salt and Light Council, a group focused on getting churches involved in right-wing politics.
Via called these groups “the usual suspects” when it comes to work like this, but noted that their power has grown in recent years.

In addition to the power players from the U.S., there was a stacked lineup of folks from the global right. Lawmakers from Peru, Uruguay, and Guatemala, all countries where CIVF has been active, were present. Also in attendance was Artur Pawlowski, a Canadian far-right pastor known for his role in the Alberta Separatist movement; Armenian evangelical activist and former politician Stepan Sargsyan; and Dutch lobbyist Henk Jan van Schothorst.
What this lineup indicates, Via says, is that the Christian far-right is interested in wielding its outsized influence in the Trump administration to impact the global stage.

“It is the traction that the Christian nationalists have gained since Trump has been in office,” she says. “Because of the administration’s willingness to wield power and influence in other countries based on this Biblical worldview … you have had some political leaders be more accepting of the idea.”

In her interview for The Washington Stand, Huber said that the point of the core group is to organize concrete action towards the goals of the GCD, which on its own is a non-binding agreement with no mechanism to enforce or ensure compliance among its signatories.

One way the core group should achieve that, Huber says, is through Protego, a project launched in 2023 by IWH that creates a road map for countries to follow in their policymaking on issues of women’s health. Outlined in their Women’s Optimal Health Framework, IWH advocates against abortion and promotes sex education that prioritizes abstinence and “prepar[ing] for a healthy marriage and future family.”

While the 62-page guide makes no explicit mention of LGBTQ people, Sjödin says that this kind of sex education, which has been widely criticized as ineffective, “is focused on promoting heterosexuality as the only form of acceptable sexuality.”

“It is used to push these binary norms that are harmful for anyone who doesn’t live up to it or doesn’t agree with it, and it limits access to education for young people who need to know both about themselves, especially if they don’t think of themselves as heterosexual, but also about everyone else so that they have an understanding that humans are different.”
Giammattei speaking at an IWH conference in 2021. Screenshot via the Government of Guatemala YouTube.

A few countries have already adopted Protego’s framework. Guatemala was the first, establishing a partnership with Huber and the IWH in June 2023 under the leadership of far-right then-president Alejandro Giammattei. The Protego project worked with the country’s Ministries of Health, Education and Social Development and developed a “Parent Child Communication Guide” that would promote IWH’s narratives on sex and family planning to Guatemalans.
Huber claims the guide, which was spread throughout the country via partnerships with influencers and faith and business leaders, has reached 3 million school-aged children in Guatemala.
Huber and Ugandan First Lady Janet Museveni signing the agreement of their partnership on Protego in 2024. Screenshot via UBC Television Uganda YouTube.

Uganda, where gay sex is punishable by death, was the next country to adopt the framework in early 2024. Unlike in Guatemala, specific details have been difficult to access and not publicly shared, but promoting abstinence-only sex education has been a publicly stated priority.
Other countries, including Hungary and Burundi, have also signaled their support for Protego, but less is known about their actions on the matter.
While the new core group has not yet been officially established, statements by Lara and Huber suggest an intention to do so in the near future.

“[It will take] less time than people assume, because the hardest part is already done,” Huber said in her Washington Stand interview. “The coalition exists. The shared commitments are on paper and have held through changes of government in multiple countries.”
Ipas, in its briefing, emphasizes that there is still a way to go before the core group’s establishment and cautions advocates to “avoid overstating [its] legitimacy and power.”
However, Sjödin warns that the plans, and the danger they present, must be taken seriously.

“Currently, we are seeing quite an extensive and horrendous backlash against LGBTQ+ people,” she says. “What they potentially want to do here is to actually make inclusion of everyone more difficult.”

articles.title: How an extremist network articulated a hoax linking Brazil’s President Lula to child abuse on X
articles.author: Fernanda Canofre
paras: Monitoring of 1,819 posts showed far-right users tried to manipulate Grok, X’s AI tool
Originally published on Global Voices
Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva. Art by: Méuri Elle/Aos Fatos, used with permission.

This article was originally published on the fact-checking agency Aos Fatos website, on September 30, 2026. It is part of the joint initiative Laboratório de Investigação Eleitoral (Investigative Electoral Lab) with Agência Pública, Amado Mundo and Núcleo Jornalismo. An edited version is republished here under a partnership agreement between Global Voices and Pública.

A few days before the first round of the 2026 general elections in Brazil on October 4, it took only a few hours for a line said by President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva about preventive exams for prostate cancer to be twisted into a pedophilia accusation against him. Aos Fatos obtained and checked 1,819 posts on X (formerly Twitter), which reconstructed how this hoax was planted and harvested by Bolsonarista users on social media between September 28 and 29.

The distortion in the meaning of Lula’s speech stemmed from a false pedophilia accusation that had already been boosted hours ahead of a statement he made at a campaign event in the city of Belém, Pará state, on September 28. Users manipulated questions asked to Grok, X’s AI assistance tool, to make it state “Lula consumes CP” — an acronym in English for child pornography.
The chatbot warned that the sentence was wordplay and that it had no records to support the claim. However, the edit cut from Lula’s speech, shared on social media, gave the narrative new momentum.

Besides requests to make the video viral and to mobilize influencers, some publications also revived old episodes and characters without any connection to Lula’s line to back theories associating the president with child abuse.

During his rally, Lula was talking about the importance of cancer prevention and criticizing men’s resistance to having prostate exams, compared to women’s healthcare culture, which, according to him, is used to having gynecological exams from an early age.

Among the publications with broader reach identified by the survey, one of the first to cut a quote from Lula’s speech was posted at 11.59 p.m. on September 28 by Pâm, an influencer, founder of a Bolsonarista site called The Incorrupt, and member of Estúdio 5, a pro-Bolsonaro content-making hub aligned with Catholicism.
A user identified as Pâm posted: ‘Lula saying women ‘learn to be touched ever since they are little’ WHAT THE FUCK, PRESIDENT? Are you NUTS???.’ Image: Screenshot from X. Fair use.

At 12.28 a.m. on September 29, the Space Liberdade account published another cut from the same quote. It took only a minute for the interpretation to be turned into an explicit accusation. At 12.29 a.m., two other posts were already calling the president “a pedophile”; one of them requesting users to pass this claim along.

In the following hours, several users started acting to amplify the reach of the accusation. Posts asked people to download and repost the video, suggested boosting the hashtag #LULAPEDOPHILE, and included messages like “it has to go viral.” At 2.48 a.m., a profile proposed to pick out two sentences from Lula’s speech, create a hashtag, and mobilize 10 to 20 influencers around it.

An account called Space Liberdade posted: ‘URGENT — Lula says men don’t like ‘to be touched’ and states that women learn ‘to be touched’ since they are little. (…) a man doesn’t; he doesn’t know that once he has prostate cancer they will touch him a lot.’ Image: Screenshot from X. Fair use.

Five hours before Pâm’s publication, users connected to the so-called “bolha da resenha” (hangout banter bubble) were already experimenting with Grok, forcing the tool to associate Lula with pedophilia. The term describes an ecosystem of profiles, most of them anonymous, that combine aggressive humour, extremist political content, and reproducing chans aesthetics — anonymous forums well known as one of the main cradles of the current far-right.

One of the first users started with the words “cerveja e picanha” (beer and filet steak) and asked the tool to summarize the expression with its initials in two letters, manipulating it to write “Lula consumes CP” (child pornography). After that, other profiles set new instructions and made the chatbot create similar sentences.

The stories crossed paths overnight. At 3.39 a.m., a user shared a cut with the line about “touch” and asked Grok if Lula was “addicted to CP.” At 4.10 a.m., another one reloaded the association in a comment on Space Liberdade’s post.

The survey also found references to codes like “Jack” and “CPzeiro,” besides slogans such as “PROTECT OUR CHILDREN” and “LULA DON’T TOUCH OUR CHILDREN.” Overall, 43 percent of the posts analyzed (746) had straightforward pedophilia accusations or, besides accusing Lula, encouraged the propagation of this assumption.
Poster widely shared on social media featuring a girl and the message: ‘Lula, leave our children at peace!’ Image: Screenshot from X. Fair use.

The narrative was already formed by the time it reached profiles with major political prominence. At 9.49 a.m. on September 29, Nikolas Ferreira, a die-hard Jair Bolsonaro ally and member of the Chamber of Deputies, published one of the cuts. At 10.23 a.m., he shared a video playing Lula’s quote and saying: “A little girl doesn’t learn to be touched in any way, Lula!!!”
Ferreira had been linked to the “hangout banter bubble” before.

In September 2025, after the killing of conservative US activist Charlie Kirk, members of the group celebrated Ferreira’s posts saying he had “joined the hangout.” At the time, the politician published a version of the Pepe the Frog meme, a channer mascot, featuring his own image and saying “Be the far-right that they fear.”

The survey doesn’t indicate that the Congressman had taken part in these recent experiments with Grok or in creating the accusation against Lula. Yet he shows up among the first politicians with a wider reach to boost the narrative, hours after it started circulating.

A while after Ferreira’s posts, expressions associated with this narrative were among X’s trending topics. “PROTECT THE CHILDREN,” which was ranked 28th at 9.04 a.m., jumped to the first spot by 11.15 a.m. At the same time, “LULA DON’T TOUCH THE CHILDREN” was in fourth, and “pedophile” in 20th.

On September 30, the Superior Electoral Court (TSE) gave Nikolas Ferreira a 24-hour deadline to remove his post on X. Minister Estela Aranha argued that he had attributed an “entirely different connotation” to the original quote, taking it out of the public health context and associating it with crimes.
From misinformation to conspiracy

After it went viral, the hoax no longer relied on what was said in Belém. Social media accounts started to revive episodes and characters without any connection to it to introduce Lula as a member of an alleged pedophile network or ring.

These theories also reached Telegram and WhatsApp groups monitored by Aos Fatos. Besides claiming Lula had defended or “trivialized” pedophilia in his speech, messages started to talk about a “likely inclination to pedophilia” and to introduce isolated episodes as an indication of such behaviour.

One of the allegations exploited the fact that the speech took place in the state of Pará, where several cases of sexual violence against children had allegedly occurred in the local Marajó archipelago. “A geographical and discursive coincidence that should, at least, cause embarrassment rather than applause,” read one of the messages.

There is no evidence linking Lula to such crimes registered in the region. Sexual violence against children and teens is a real and documented problem, but it has also been a target of false and unsubstantiated allegations for years. Some of the posts included statements made in 2022 by Senator Damares Alves, then minister of women, family, and human rights in Bolsonaro’s cabinet, saying she had been attacked for denouncing abuses in Marajó Island.
At the time, Alves said she had received testimonies about children who had had their teeth removed to facilitate oral sex and were forced to ingest pasty food to facilitate anal sex.

The allegations weren’t registered by any investigative bodies, and the Federal Prosecution Office (MPF) presented a public civil action against Alves for spreading what they classified as “sensationalist false information involving sexual abuse and torture to the children of Marajó.”

Some posts also started to associate Lula with Jeffrey Epstein, the disgraced US financier accused of leading a network of sexual exploitation involving minors. What was used as evidence for that was an email attributed to Epstein in which he claims to have talked to Lula on the phone, during the time Lula was imprisoned in Curitiba, Brazil, through Noam Chomsky.

The email exists, but it doesn’t prove whether the conversation ever occurred. Valeria Chomsky, Noam’s wife, denied he had mediated it. When the email was first publicized, the Social Communications Office of the Presidency said that “the referred phone call never happened.” This kind of phone call would also be incompatible with the rules of the Federal Police prison ward where Lula was held, according to experts interviewed by Folha de S. Paulo newspaper.
Other Brazilian politicians were also mentioned by Epstein, including former president Jair Bolsonaro, whom the financier referred to once as “the man.”

articles.title: Hong Kong police launch AI-powered national security platform for school pupils
articles.author: Hong Kong Free Press
paras: ‘May the seeds of national security take root and sprout in the hearts of the pupils…’
Originally published on Global Voices
Hong Kong police launch an AI-powered national security education platform for the city’s pupils during a ceremony on October 6, 2026. Photo: HKPF, via Facebook. Used with permission.

This article was originally published by Hong Kong Free Press on October 13, 2026. The following version is republished on Global Voices under a content partnership agreement. It is also part of Global Voices’ October 2026 Spotlight series, “Big Tech and Authoritarianism.” You can support this coverage by donating here.
Hong Kong police have launched an artificial intelligence-powered national security education platform for young students.

The NSmarties AI Interactive Platform was officially launched on October 6, 2026, at a ceremony at Precious Blood Primary School in Ap Lei Chau, with about 700 pupils attending, police said in a Facebook post:

【 NSmarties童心護港AI互動平台 • 正式啟動 】 國家安全，由童心出發！ 由警務處國家安全處主辦的「NSmarties童心護港AI互動平台」今日（6日）於海怡寶血小學正式啟動！ 警務處處長周一鳴、警務處副處長（國家安全）江學禮、寶血會總會長區綺雯修女等一眾嘉賓，聯同約700位同學一同見證這個重要時刻。 啟動禮圓滿結束，標誌着國安教育以創新科技走進校園的新里程！ 願國安種子在同學心裏生根發芽，茁壯成長！

[ NSmarties: Children’s Hearts Protect Hong Kong AI Interactive Platform • Officially Launched ] National security begins with the hearts of children! Organized by the National Security Department of the Hong Kong Police Force, the ‘NSmarties: Children’s Hearts Protect Hong Kong AI Interactive Platform’ was officially launched today (6th) at Sea View Precious Blood Primary School! Distinguished guests, including Commissioner of Police Joe Chow Yat-ming, Deputy Commissioner of Police (National Security) Kelvin Kong Hok-lai, and Sister Au Yee-man, President of the Precious Blood Society, joined some 700 pupils in witnessing this momentous occasion. The successful launch ceremony marks a new milestone in bringing national security education into schools through innovative technology! May the seeds of national security take root and sprout in the hearts of the pupils, and grow strong!

The platform, jointly developed by police and Hong Kong Qianfan Technology, lets students generate personalized stories centered on China’s “holistic approach to national security” — a framework pushed by Chinese President Xi Jinping that covers areas from politics and the economy to ecology and technology.
It also features the voices of Chow and security chief Chris Tang, who explain the city’s national security laws and security information.
The ceremony marked a “milestone” in bringing national security education into the city’s schools through innovative technologies, police said.
The NSmarties platform was first unveiled on National Security Education Day in April, but it was not fully launched to the public at that time.
Hong Kong has strengthened national security education alongside a crackdown since Beijing imposed a national security law in 2020 following the 2019 protests and unrest.

Beijing inserted national security legislation directly into Hong Kong’s mini-constitution in June 2020 following a year of pro-democracy protests and unrest. It criminalized subversion, secession, collusion with foreign forces and terrorist acts — broadly defined to include disruption to transport and other infrastructure. The move gave police sweeping new powers and led to hundreds of arrests amid new legal precedents, while dozens of civil society groups disappeared. The authorities say it restored stability and peace to the city, rejecting criticism from trade partners, the UN and NGOs.

articles.title: The mafia isn’t keeping fentanyl out of Europe – the lack of demand is
articles.author: Anna Sergi, Professor of Sociology of Law and Deviance, Università di Bologna; University of Essex; The University of Melbourne
paras: Fentanyl and other synthetic opioids are still the single biggest driver of overdose deaths in the US. They were involved in around 38,000 of the roughly 70,000 deaths recorded in 2025, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.

Europe’s figures are of a different order. In 16 countries that reported data, fentanyl and its derivatives were linked to a total of around 210 drug-induced deaths in 2024, up from about 130 in 2023. Most of that rise may involve medicines rather than illicitly made fentanyl.

Other potent synthetic opioids, notably nitazenes, have driven recent peaks in deaths in several countries. In Italy, the government’s latest report on addiction counted only five fentanyl-related deaths in 2025.
This gap has prompted a striking explanation: that Italy’s mafias, wary of a drug that kills their customers and draws police attention, have chosen to keep fentanyl out.

It is a compelling story. But it does not fit what we know about drug markets or mafias. Europe’s comparatively low fentanyl numbers are better explained by something less cinematic: there is very little demand for it.
Crisis built on prescriptions

America’s fentanyl crisis was largely manufactured and a result of entrenched corruption. From the late 1990s, aggressively marketed prescription painkillers such as OxyContin were handed out widely, with their addictive potential played down. Millions of people developed opioid dependence through entirely legal channels.

When access was tightened in the 2010s, that dependence did not disappear. People turned to the illicit market: first heroin, then fentanyl, which is cheap to make, easy to smuggle and so potent that tiny amounts go a long way. Drug trafficking groups from Mexico that already supplied heroin to the US simply added a new product to their range.

Europe never had an equivalent prescription wave. Opioid painkillers are prescribed far more cautiously there, so there was no large population suddenly cut off from a legal supply and looking for a substitute.

Heroin, meanwhile, never went away. It is still Europe’s most commonly used illicit opioid, according to the EU Drugs Agency. Most of it has historically come from Afghanistan, entering Europe through the Balkans, and the market has proved resilient and stable.

Even as Afghan opium cultivation collapsed after the Taliban banned it in 2000, and then issued a second ban after returning to power in 2022, stockpiles and production elsewhere have kept supply flowing.

People who use heroin in Europe have established habits, networks and treatment services built around it. There is no obvious reason for them to switch to an unfamiliar drug, and no mass of new users being pushed towards one.

The veto argument also rests on a picture of organised crime as one strategic group, able to weigh up a product and rule it out across a whole country. But that is not how Italian mafias work, and it is not how drug markets work.

Crime groups such as the ‘Ndrangheta are made up of families, clans and individuals who act on opportunity, shaped by local structures and contacts. They broker, invest and supply where there is money to be made.
Nobody inside one organisation can impose a marketwide ban, let alone across the different mafias and the many other organised crime groups active in Europe’s drug trade.

Nor are Italian mafias squeamish about dangerous drugs. Their central role in Europe’s cocaine trade is well documented, and has been a focus of my own research. But more crucially, their adaptation to changing markets is their distinguishing factor.
Two recent cases from Calabria, the ‘Ndrangheta’s home region, say more about where Italy’s drug economy is heading.

Police are uncovering more, and larger, cannabis plantations hidden in the region’s mountains. In early October, police found ten plantations with more than 4,500 plants in woodland around Caulonia, San Luca and Roghudi. The sites were reachable only on foot and fitted with drip irrigation and automatic timers.

Months earlier, in May, law enforcement found a clandestine cocaine refinery in the countryside of Sant'Agata del Bianco, with hydraulic presses and more than 500kg of cutting agents. The investigation points to a transnational network of South American and Italian traffickers, with its own chemist, rather than a ‘Ndrangheta operation.
Both cases point the same way. Italy’s drug economy is not a closed shop run by one or two organisations. Independent operators can set up there, process product locally and serve European demand.

The idea of a mafia that protects its customers hands criminal groups a reputation for order and restraint they have not earned. It also distracts from where the risks actually lie. Europe’s opioid market is becoming more complex and potent: new synthetic opioids such as nitazenes are already in circulation.

The answer to that is not to wait for a mafia decision. It is better drug monitoring, early-warning systems, drug-checking services and making naloxone, the opioid overdose antidote, easy to get hold of. Europe’s fentanyl story so far is a story about demand. Keeping it that way is a public health job, not a criminal one.

articles.title: Prime’s Carrie miniseries expands Stephen King’s story – but weakens its central horror
articles.author: Ahmed Honeini, Honorary Research Associate in American Literature, Royal Holloway, University of London
paras: Warning: this article contains spoilers for those not familiar with the plot of Stephen King’s Carrie.

Amazon Prime’s Carrie is the fourth screen adaptation of Stephen King’s debut novel. Developed by frequent King collaborator Mike Flanagan (who also directed Gerald’s Game, Doctor Sleep and The Life of Chuck), this eight-episode miniseries follows the legacy of Brian De Palma’s classic 1976 film starring Sissy Spacek.
Published in 1974, King’s original book tells the story of the infamous “black prom” through a tense, tight mix of prose, fake news reports and eyewitness interviews.

Bullied teenager Carrie White, who lives alone with her religious zealot mother in a quiet Maine town, discovers that she has supernatural, telekinetic powers (the ability to manipulate matter with her mind). After being invited to the senior prom by high school heartthrob Tommy Ross, she finally has a chance to escape her mother’s influence and find acceptance among her peers. But when events at prom take a dramatic, horrific turn, Carrie’s powers are finally unleashed.

In the first few episodes, Flanagan is surprisingly faithful to King’s novel. He also usefully deepens the moral complexity behind much of the story’s events. Chris Hargensen, Carrie’s nemesis, is developed beyond being simply villainous and cold-hearted. Instead, she is shown to be as troubled and afflicted by social and parental pressure as Carrie is herself.

The performances of the central cast are excellent. Summer H. Howell as Carrie, Alison Thornton as Chris and Siena Agudong as their mutual friend Sue Snell are standouts. And Flanagan’s aesthetic flourishes are, at times, masterful. A montage in the penultimate episode set to Lana Del Rey’s song Did You Know There’s a Tunnel Under Ocean Blvd showcases the lead-up to and arrival at prom that evokes both adolescent wonderment and anxious dread at the events about to unfold.
However, Flanagan’s expansion of the novel’s events are also this adaptation’s fundamental weaknesses.

The original novel and the classic film adaptation are tightly structured and compact. The Prime mini series, meanwhile, stretches events over the course of eight nearly hour-long episodes. The novel’s brevity – it’s just over 200 pages in most editions – compounds the claustrophobic atmosphere of the intense bullying Carrie suffers, which makes the tragedy of the black prom even more acute.

Crucially, the novel and film also keep Carrie isolated from Chris, Sue and the other girls at school, whereas Flanagan depicts Carrie forming an unlikely friendship with them even after they begin bullying her. This alteration makes little narrative sense especially given that, in the novel, the prom is depicted as the climax of Carrie’s young life and a moment of burgeoning, long-deferred social acceptance.

Flanagan’s major error is in his creation of an entirely new character, Emaline (Thalia Dudek), a fellow telekinetic who negatively influences Carrie’s behaviour. Emaline encourages Carrie to not only hone and strengthen her powers but to strike back at her bullies.

To my mind, this change undermines the entire point of King’s novel and diminishes precisely why the story continues to be so powerful after more than half a century: the black prom is the moment at which Carrie finally exerts agency, control and power over her tormentors. To take that power away from her is a morally neat and misguided attempt at clearing Carrie of wrongdoing. It undermines the implication in the original novel that, perhaps, Carrie’s actions can be understood if not condoned or justified.

In a post-Columbine context where school massacres are common across the US, the implication that Carrie’s actions during the prom could be comprehensible was probably too unpalatable and divisive for the studio.

Carrie shares many similarities with King’s 1977 novel Rage (originally published under his alias, Richard Bachman). It has been permanently taken out of print by King himself after the novel was linked to several real-life high school shootings.

When seen in that context, updating these details of Carrie’s original plot allows Flanagan to approach difficult material with sensitivity. Yet, if the subject matter raises such uncomfortable questions, would viewers not benefit from a new story that, while heavily inspired by King’s original tale, makes its own unique narrative contribution to the horror genre?
Overall, Flanagan’s Carrie fails to satisfy as much as the original novel or 1976 film adaptation do, which is unfortunate, because the series shines when it is most faithful to the source material.

Flanagan shared in an interview that King’s first response to plans for a new adaptation was: “Leave her [Carrie] alone. She’s been through enough.” Carrie, and the audience, may have been better served if Flanagan had taken the author’s advice.

articles.title: Japan’s MMX mission aims to swipe soil samples from Mars’ moon Phobos
articles.author: Daniel Brown, Lecturer in Astronomy, Nottingham Trent University
paras: A Japanese space mission is about to launch towards Mars. But it will not land on the planet itself. Instead, the Martian Moons Exploration (MMX) mission will focus on Phobos, the bigger of Mars’s two small moons.
The mission will lift off on Monday October 19 at 20:41 BST on an H3 rocket from the Tanegashima Space Center, in the south of Japan.

This will start a five-year mission, during which the spacecraft will orbit and explore Phobos, deploy a lander, touch down and collect soil and small pebbles. In a world first, these samples will be delivered to Earth for study in laboratories.

MMX is led by the Japanese Aerospace Exploration Agency (Jaxa), in collaboration with the US, France, Germany and the European Space Agency (Esa). The overall science objective is to unravel the origins of the two Martian moons, the smaller of which is called Deimos. Mission scientists also want to examine the wider evolution of Mars and its local environment in space.
We still have no clear understanding of how the red planet got its moons. These natural satellites could have been hapless asteroids that were passing by Mars when they got captured by its gravity.

Another possibility is that that they formed when an asteroid collided with Mars, causing rocky material to be thrown out into space. Gradually, this material coalesced into Phobos and Deimos. The MMX mission will give us Phobos’s chemical composition, which could help distinguish between theories.

Grabbing samples from Phobos will be no easy task, however. Russia tried this in 2011 with its Phobos Grunt mission. The spacecraft launched successfully to low Earth orbit, but failed to fire its engines to send it toward Mars.

However, Jaxa is well placed to succeed. The space agency has already proved that it can return samples from asteroids with its Hayabusa space missions, which lasted from 2003-10 (Hayabusa) and 2018-20 (Hayabusa 2).

MMX will trial sophisticated sampling techniques designed for Phobos’s low gravity. The moon has about 0.1% the gravitational pull that Earth does. This means that a human on Phobos could jump a distance of 1.5 km horizontally without much effort.

The mission will also be a test of communication between the spacecraft and a newly developed ground station. After launch and deployment, MMX will take a year to reach Mars, arriving in August 2027. It will first circle the red planet before slipping into orbit around Phobos about a month later.

The spacecraft consists of three modules with distinct functions: a propulsion module to get MMX into orbit around Mars, an exploration module with landing and sample collection gear and a return module to deliver the sample to Earth.

The mission will make use of 13 science instruments to explore Phobos. High resolution cameras called Tengoo and Orochi will map the surface and a laser altimeter (Lidar) will build up a picture of the moon’s contours. Lidar uses laser pulses to measure the distance from the spacecraft to features on the surface.

An infrared spectrograph called MIRS will survey Phobos’s minerals, while a gamma ray and neutron detector, called Megane, will determine the moon’s elemental composition. From a greater distance, MMX will also gather data on Mars’s smaller moon Deimos.
The instruments will send back data that controllers will use to decide where and how to land the spacecraft on Phobos.

In early 2029, the MMX exploration module will deploy a small microwave oven-sized rover called Idefix, which has been developed jointly by Jaxa, the French space agency Cnes and the German Aerospace Center (DLR). Idefix will drop down onto Phobos’ surface from between 40 and 100m in altitude.

The rover will then right itself and travel over the surface during an operational period expected to last about 100 days. It will be using several sensors, including a Raman spectrometer and radiometer, to make a final call about where the exploration module should land.

In 2030, the module will swoop down and land on Phobos, remaining on its surface for about 2.5 hours. It will be able to extract samples from the surface once or possibly twice by landing again at a different location. The ability to sample from more than one place on Phobos is vital to understanding the moon’s composition.

The exploration module will use either an instrument called the C-sampler to drill a core or a device knowns as the P-sampler, which blows a jet of nitrogen gas to blast soil and loose pebbles off the surface and into a sample collection chamber.

The C-sampler would be able to collect a core from up to 2cm below the surface. This would provide the mission with a sample composition unaltered by solar radiation, which causes chemical changes to planetary surfaces over time. The P-sampler is a back-up option, but carries some small risk of toppling the spacecraft in low gravitational fields like the one on Phobos.

Having gathered at least 10 grams of material, the spacecraft will leave the Martian moon, separating from its landing gear. It will then travel back to Earth, arriving in 2031. On its approach, the spacecraft will eject its sample probe, which will then descend through Earth’s atmosphere. It will land using parachutes in Australia, where it will be recovered and transported to Japan.

A potential side-benefit of the mission is that samples from Phobos might also include material from Mars. Phobos closely orbits the red planet and is thought to be constantly hoovering up Martian soil. This soil is thought to be regularly ejected from the planet’s surface by asteroid impacts.

MMX could therefore be considered a lite-version of the Mars Sample Return (MSR) mission. MSR, a collaboration between the US and European space agencies, would have sent rock samples from the Martian surface to Earth. However, budgetary pressures led to the programme being effectively cancelled by US Congress.
If scientists get lucky with the samples from MMX, they might get a nice consolation prize.

articles.title: Peru’s Indigenous people in Cutivireni and Oviri take the front line against Amazon wildfires
articles.author: Cool Earth
paras: Indigenous guardians play a critical role in protecting the land, their homes, and their livelihoods
Originally published on Global Voices

The Cool Earth initiative in Cutivireni and Oviri works around three key concepts: the monitoring of satellite fire weather alerts, the introduction of a flag-based system regarding safe times to conduct traditional fire practices, and practical training to contain small blazes and prevent them from causing devastation to the Indigenous people in the rainforest. Photo by Cool Earth, 2026; used with permission.

It’s September and 2026 has already been defined by wildfires spanning across the globe. Driven by the heat and dryness of the climate crisis, outbursts on the edge of Bordeaux, France have forced 200,000 from their homes and led to deaths in Spain. Smoke has billowed across the Canada-U.S. border, covering cities in smog.

Fires are expected to continue as seasons transition in the Southern Hemisphere, with a severe El Niño phenomenon that the United Nations warns will add pressure to an already scorching globe, risking similar conditions to those that — back in 2024 — drove the worst Amazonian wildfires in two decades.

With fire and drought risks set to increase in the coming months, Indigenous people in the Amazon rainforest are stepping up to take on new roles as fire brigade members, protecting both their homes and a key natural resource in the fight against climate change.

Ahead of this year’s El Niño weather pattern, Indigenous people from Peru’s Cutivireni and Oviri communities approached Cool Earth: they wanted to ensure they were equipped to fight any fires this coming season. The organization’s long-established relationship with the two Indigenous groups and experience working with the Central Asháninka of the Ene River to create the Paamari programme, made it easier to establish four fire crews across communities that were already springing into action.

In Cutivireni, the newly formed Chullachaqui fire crew have faced multiple blazes. Named after an Amazonian forest spirit, the crew understand the critical role they play in protecting the land, their homes, and their livelihoods. In early August came one of the first tests of their training: alerted by people in the Tsyapo and Pajonal communities, community brigade members joined up with their partners in Central Cutivireni to tackle the fire, which they successfully put out.

Julio Acosta, Cool Earth’s Forest Data Manager, said that the organization really admires and appreciates how the communities have been making the best use of what they have been building with them, adding, “This early action taken in Tsyapo and Pajonal demonstrates how effectively they put into practice what they’ve learned in the workshops.”

The training was taken directly from concepts in the Paamari programme. Similar to Paamari, the Cool Earth initiative with Cutivireni and Oviri works around three key concepts: the increased monitoring of satellite fire weather alerts, the introduction of a flag-based system regarding safe times to conduct traditional fire practices, and practical training to contain small blazes and prevent them from causing devastation to the Indigenous people in the rainforest.

The communities themselves often act as the brigade’s eyes, alerting them to smoke or flames. Working in close coordination with local authorities, brigade members first assess the wildfires and try to tame the blazes in their initial stage, before they require a more complex response by the authorities.

Acosta stressed the importance of highlighting the fact that the main work of these brigades lies in prevention, rather than initial response. “This tends to be less visible,” he explained, {but the measures they take, such as the flag system, help reduce the occurrence of these fires. Seeing the initiative and eagerness to learn more from the brigade members motivates us to expand and improve the work we’ve been implementing together.”

Along with protecting their homes, the Indigenous communities act as custodians of the rainforest — a vital global asset for fighting the climate crisis. According to the World Resources Institute, rainforests provide 23 percent of the climate mitigation needed to help stabilise global temperatures. Their destruction from wildfires depletes the world’s natural carbon stores and also releases tons of carbon back into the atmosphere.

At the moment, not every fire can be tackled. August saw a fire in Cutivireni that reached a score of three out of five on Peru’s national disaster response. When interviewed, onlookers noted that there was “little that’s left or [that] survived.” The fire raged for four days and went on to destroy 50 hectares of land – about the size 70 football pitches.

With communities set to come under more strain, Cool Earth hopes to establish further training, turning the initiative into a fully fledged project. Providing Indigenous people with more finance and training capabilities, they hope to meet the ever-growing demand for wildfire training in the Peruvian Amazon.

articles.title: How authoritarian states are building an international market for digital surveillance
articles.author: Daria Dergacheva
paras: The main danger of AI in authoritarian regimes is the ability to suppress any protest
Originally published on Global Voices

Moscow subway cameras are connected to a facial recognition system. Screenshot taken from the YouTube video “Facial recognition cameras help detain dissidents in the Moscow metro” by the DW YouTube channel; fair use.

This post is part of Global Voices’ October 2026 Spotlight series, “Big Tech and Authoritarianism.” In this Spotlight, we explore how Big Tech facilitates and hinders authoritarian governments and practices, and how these choices influence the Global South. You can support this coverage by donating here.

Sonya, from Stavropol Krai, Russia, is 15 years old. In June 2026, she was sentenced to 70 hours of compulsory labor, connected to a February 2026 incident in which she had written the surname “Navalny” on a bus stop. That stop happened to be in a district that was being monitored by officers from the Center for Combating Extremism, commonly called Center E. Similarly, Yuri, a pensioner from Astrakhan who was also identified from surveillance footage, was given three years of restricted freedom for writing “No to War” in red marker on buildings.

Authoritarian regimes are increasingly using artificial intelligence (AI) as a technology of political survival. Cameras with facial recognition, video analytics, biometric databases, digital IDs, social media monitoring, Deep Packet Inspection (DPI) systems, and public service platforms are gradually merging into a single infrastructure of control.

Such a system makes it possible not only to observe citizens in real time, but also to reconstruct their past movements, connections, habits, communications, and political activity. The main risk is that AI and related technologies make repression faster and less visible: the state no longer needs to constantly demonstrate force if citizens know they can be identified retroactively.

Modern digital authoritarianism is not developing in isolation, but through the international exchange of technologies, standards, and practices. China, Russia, Iran, Belarus, Venezuela, countries in Africa, Western and Central Asia, and companies connected to them, sell and exchange AI infrastructure tools that are being used for the purpose of repression. Western technologies are also being bought and exchanged within authoritarian regimes.

In early June 2026, Sberbank Deputy Chairman Alexander Vedyakhin told Reuters that the company was offering countries in the Global South access to Russian AI models that would take “local values” into account. Vedyakhin was referring to specific large language models (LLMs) — GigaChat and YandexGPT — which Russia had been trying to develop since 2019.

However, as IT expert Alexander Isavnin told journalists at the podcast Zhivoy Gvozd, Russian generative AI models lag behind American and Chinese models and cannot even generate text in Cyrillic. Yet, new national and sovereign AI models are supposed to reflect traditional values, including patriotism, service to the Fatherland and responsibility for its fate, a strong family, historical memory and continuity between generations, and unity of the peoples of Russia. These models are expected to be trained on domestic, authentically Russian material.

It is reasonable to assume that in countries like those in Western Asia, Russian AI models will reflect adherence to Islamic traditions, while in Argentina, perhaps, they will reflect respect for football from an early age. Developers, meanwhile, do not understand how people with no idea about how any of this works can write AI laws: “In places, the document reads as if it was written by people who had only ever seen LLMs in local news.” From the perspective of global democracy, however, this illiteracy among Russian lawmakers suggests that Russia is unlikely to supply LLMs to autocracies around the world.

China, by contrast — unlike American developers — makes its language models open in principle, meaning that anyone can take the code and modify it for their own needs. In China, all LLMs are controlled and tightly regulated by the state, so party censorship is written into the code from the start — for example, you cannot get an answer about the Tiananmen Square protests. However, the models are distributed as open source, which is why more than 50 percent of Chinese model users come from developers, including those in the Global South.

At the same time, the U.S.-based ChatGPT can easily replicate AI-generated Iranian propaganda videos, in which the main characters are Lego figures. Only once, a France 24 investigation showed, did the chatbot alert the journalist that he might be inadvertently reproducing propaganda, but desisted when he said it was only satire.

AI also includes other tech developments, like the so-called “smart city” systems which, in the Chinese version, imply comprehensive surveillance of a state’s own citizens. This can include video surveillance, wiretapping, internet censorship, facial recognition systems, ethnic profiling, and so on. In supplying such systems to the Global South, China has overtaken Russia.

Yet, Russia is not lagging behind in the use of AI to surveil its own citizens. State media write that Moscow has long moved beyond the threshold implied by the concept of a “smart city.” Today, it includes a complex digital urban ecosystem made up of video surveillance, AI, big data, and the “internet of things.”

According to estimates by Comparitech, two of the ten cities outside China with the highest number of cameras per person are Russian: Moscow and St. Petersburg. The list also includes four Indian cities, Seoul in South Korea, Baghdad in Iraq, Kabul in Afghanistan, and Singapore. In China itself, the number of cameras has practically reached a ratio of one camera for every two people: the largest mass-surveillance system in the world.

Russia has sold, and in some cases, continues to supply its surveillance software products to other authoritarian states, while remaining technologically dependent on China. In 2024, up to 80 percent of all cameras used in Russia were made in China and sold under Russian brands.

China has built one of the most sophisticated domestic systems of digital control; it has also turned the export of digital infrastructure into part of its foreign policy via the Digital Silk Road, launched back in 2017. Through the initiative, China promotes digital infrastructure, technological cooperation, standards, and solutions for countries in Asia, Africa, and Latin America. Formally, these projects are described as support for the digital transformation of developing states, but they deepen partners’ dependence on Chinese technologies and create channels for the spread of AI systems, especially mass-surveillance technologies.

Experts from the Carnegie Endowment, the European Parliament, and Freedom House agree that the main danger of AI in authoritarian regimes is the ability to suppress any protest before it has even properly materialized. AI systems can help authorities detect early signals: unusual online activity, preparations, movement patterns, and links between activists.

All of this has, among other things, already been done in the digital Gulag that Moscow has built. As journalist Andrei Zakharov writes in his new book “Russian Cyberpunk,” Moscow authorities have been collecting comprehensive data on Muscovites since as early as 2014, and have been using AI to bring information from different agencies into a single database. After the 2021 protests, activists were arrested using facial recognition systems. According to Zakharov, in Moscow in 2023, there were already more than 220,000 video devices connected to a unified data storage and processing center.

Now, against the backdrop of sentences of ten-plus years for publishing an article in a foreign journal, for example, the sentences handed down in 2021 to people prosecuted after the so-called “Palace Case” seem small — but this was the first instance in which people in Russia were arrested as a result of video surveillance analysis. Police came to Yevgeny Yesenov’s apartment and arrested him the day after the rally; he became the first prisoner in the case and was sentenced to four years in a penal colony, though he was released on parole after a year and a half. While things like this happened in pre-war Russia, now, as a result of organized surveillance by the “smart city” system, anyone’s address can be found using their face.

After the start of the full-scale invasion of Ukraine, people were arrested in the same way for anti-war graffiti or for setting fire to military enlistment offices — any forms of protest that had been captured and analyzed by the country’s AI surveillance system.

As T-Invariant writes, Russia is also developing AI for drones and cryptography at Moscow State University under the leadership of Putin’s daughter, using Chinese and American gray-market chips and open Western AI technologies. It is also sharing such technologies with China and North Korea.

Chinese participation in “smart city” projects in Western Asia is unfolding in a region where, according to the EIU Democracy Index for 2023, 16 out of 20 territories are classified as authoritarian regimes. These projects are most highly concentrated in the Gulf states: the UAE has 11 projects, while Saudi Arabia has seven. Outside this bloc, Turkey plays the most visible role with five projects, while the remaining projects are distributed among Algeria, Egypt, Iraq, Iran, Morocco, and Tunisia.

The latest Chinese concept of the “smart city,” from 2022, involves real-time information monitoring across virtually all aspects of urban life. This technology makes it possible to establish continuous real-time digital monitoring of a city, giving the government the ability to multiply its control over citizens.
China and Russia’s links with Iran

In February 2026, research by the civil society organization Article 19 found that the architecture of internet control in Iran relies heavily on Chinese technologies. The report said that China supplied Iran with facial recognition technologies, internet filtering equipment, and surveillance tools from companies such as Huawei, ZTE, Hikvision, Tiandy, as well as smaller Chinese suppliers.

At the same time, an investigation by Le Monde and Forbidden Stories showed that Iran acquired the Russian facial recognition system FindFace, developed by NtechLab, through Iranian intermediary companies. The software was resold to entities linked to the Iranian state, including the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) and the Ministry of Intelligence.

As early as 2019, when Iranian women began receiving fines by mail for not wearing the hijab while in a car, citizens have been talking about their government’s use of digital surveillance. In December 2025, Iran and Russia signed a cooperation agreement in the fields of AI, cybersecurity, the digital economy, blockchain, fintech, and partnerships with the private sector.

Surveillance of people in authoritarian regimes is organized by both cameras and control of internet traffic. The Russian company Protei, headquartered in Jordan but rooted in St. Petersburg, has reportedly supported Iran’s efforts to introduce systems for interception, monitoring, and traffic management, as well as to integrate DPI into network architecture. Its clients include MTN Irancell, Iran’s largest telecom provider, as well as operators and government entities in Tajikistan, Uzbekistan, Pakistan, Kenya, Namibia, Qatar, and other countries.

Taraneh M., an artist living in Iran who was detained during the “Woman, Life, Freedom” protests, said that in 2022 she had prepared for the possibility of arrest by securing her devices, deleting confidential information, and setting self-destruct timers for personal chats. Nevertheless, investigators presented her with a thick dossier of her social media posts, some of which dated back five years. Although she has been released, Taraneh is now afraid to speak on the phone lest she is being monitored.
The China-Russia relationship
Although AI development in China has surpassed Russia’s, cooperation exists in the supply of Chinese technologies, as well as scientific development.

In January 2025, on the heels of Russia’s attempts to create a network of AI alliances with BRICS and other non-Western partners, Vladimir Putin instructed the Russian government and Sberbank to deepen cooperation with China, especially with regard to AI “technological research and development.”

The immediate stimulus was sanctions, Russia’s access to advanced chips and AI equipment was restricted after its invasion of Ukraine, but its dependence on China has persisted in recent years. Supplies for new servers, for example, which Russia does not manufacture, came from China through intermediary firms.

As T-Invariant discovered, however, joint developments are being conducted in two areas: training AI for drones and mass surveillance of people. In November 2025, the creation of two joint laboratories was announced: one for nano-structured optoelectronic materials and devices, and another for AI algorithms and their applications.

Russia and North Korea are cooperating in testing AI in military operations: North Korea supplies weapons that are tested in Russia’s war on Ukraine, and data that may improve North Korean systems, including AI-guided systems, is passed back to North Korea. In May 2026, North Korea tested high-precision cruise missiles and artillery systems with AI guidance.
According to analysts, “AI” likely refers to automatic target recognition and terminal-stage guidance, although the level of technological sophistication remains unclear.

Since late 2023, North Korea has supplied Russia with ballistic missiles and artillery rockets, and their use on the battlefield in Ukraine is believed to have given Pyongyang, and likely Russia, valuable operational data.
The China-Venezuela-Belarus triangle

In Venezuela, authoritarian digital control is being built through international supply chains. Regimes do not necessarily create such systems themselves. Instead, they buy cameras, servers, video analytics platforms, DPI systems, algorithms, and software, often from countries also experiencing digital authoritarianism.

China’s Dahua, despite being added to the U.S. Entity List in 2019 because of its involvement in repression in Xinjiang, retained access to the Venezuelan market and discussed the integration of AI into surveillance systems with the authorities. Possible participation by Huawei, ZTE, and China CAMC in projects is also mentioned, although their role remains unspecified.

Between 2021 and 2023, the Venezuelan interior ministry also held talks with the Belarusian company Synesis, which is under U.S. sanctions for technologies that Belarusian authorities used to identify and arrest protesters. The Kipod software offered to Venezuela included facial recognition; searches for specific people and routes; license plate recognition; detection of weapons, abandoned objects, smoke, and crowds; perimeter control; and monitoring of traffic violations.
Countries on the African continent

A 2026 Institute of Development Studies (IDS) report on surveillance in “smart cities” in Africa showed the spread of Chinese AI-surveillance systems in 11 countries, including Algeria, Egypt, Kenya, Rwanda, Senegal, and Zimbabwe.

Carnegie’s study on the global use of AI in human surveillance predicted that the adoption of such technologies in Africa is likely to grow. Chinese exports of surveillance systems are being used in authoritarian contexts — including in Uganda and Myanmar, often through companies such as Huawei, Hikvision, and Dahua.
As in Western Asia, China-Africa cooperation in AI may look like assistance in developing “smart cities,” but its repressive use is connected with control over citizens.

Governments in Central Asia have actively purchased Chinese digital public-security systems. A report by the Caspian Policy Center says that in 2013, Tajikistan cooperated with Huawei to create a safe city surveillance system in Dushanbe worth about 22 million USD, largely financed by a Chinese loan.

Other publications note that Chinese companies occupy leading positions in “safe” and “smart city” projects across Eurasia, especially because the region offers relatively open markets for Chinese technologies.

Chinese censorship systems and related tools have also appeared in Kazakhstan, Pakistan, and Ethiopia, but cooperation between China and Central Asia mainly represents the export of AI surveillance technologies under the rhetoric of crime prevention.

Even supposedly democratic states have employed surveillance technologies to spy on their citizens. One of the most functional proposals to hinder the development of such authoritarian digital tools is to make Western technologies open source, and move digital strategies away from sovereignty and towards inclusion of the majority world : not as territories of extraction for the energy and water to run powerful data centers that serving Western AI models, but as actual participants in digital strategies and AI governance.

Such an approach would include sustainable development and practical concerns like agriculture, healthcare, education, transport, urban planning, adaptation to climate change, and many more human-centered priorities.

articles.title: Replacing just 10% of ultra-processed foods with whole foods linked to drop in bowel cancer rate
articles.author: Erikka Loftfield, Group Leader, QIMR Berghofer
paras: Replacing 10% of your intake of ultra-processed foods with minimally processed foods is linked with 2% lower incidence of bowel cancer, according to our new analysis of data from more than 460,000 US adults.
However, we also found no association between total ultra-processed food intake and bowel cancer incidence.

That said, intake of wholegrains, fibre, dairy, and calcium from ultra-processed food sources was associated with lower bowel cancer incidence. Eating ultra-processed meats was associated with higher bowel cancer incidence.
Ultra-processed foods includes things such as store-bought biscuits, instant noodles, sugary drinks, processed meats and chips.
Overall, our findings suggest the label “ultra-processed” alone doesn’t tell the full story about bowel cancer risk. What’s in the food seems to matter.
Choosing wholegrains and limiting processed meat aligns with current evidence-based guidance.
Researchers and policymakers should avoid treating all ultra-processed foods as one group as this may mask differences linked to disease risk.
Higher intakes of wholegrains, fibre, dairy, and calcium and lower intakes of processed and red meat have been associated with lower bowel cancer risk.
Importantly, these food groups and nutrients are in lots of foods, from minimally processed to ultra-processed (as defined by the Nova classification system).

Prior studies evaluating the association between ultra-processed food intake and bowel cancer risk have been inconsistent. Some have found that higher intake is associated with higher bowel cancer incidence, while others have found no association.
To find out more, we looked to a large data set from the US.
We analysed data from over 460,000 US adults who were between the ages of 50 and 71 and cancer-free when they enrolled in the NIH-AARP Diet and Health Study in 1995-96.
Participants answered questions about demographics, health conditions, and lifestyle factors, including smoking, physical activity and dietary intake.
We used data on eating frequency and portion size to estimate the daily amount of ultra-processed food each participant usually consumed.

We defined ultra-processed food using the Nova classification system. This system assigns foods and beverages into one of four groups according to the nature, extent, and purpose of industrial processing:
Group 1 contains unprocessed or minimally processed foods. It includes raw fruits and vegetables, seeds, eggs, milk, and unprocessed meat such as steak.
Group 2 contains processed culinary ingredients, including oils, butter and sugar.

Group 3 contains processed foods that are made by combining items from groups 1 and 2. This includes things such as vegetables preserved in brine and whole fruit preserved in syrup, as well as home baked breads and cured meats.

Group 4 contains ultra-processed foods, which are created using ingredients, like synthetic emulsifiers, or techniques (such as extrusion) that aren’t available to home cooks. This include things such as soft drinks, packaged snacks, mass produced breads, fruit yoghurt, hotdogs and ready-to-eat meals.

The food frequency questionnaire was not designed to assess processing. So, we evaluated how well the questionnaire measured ultra-processed food intake in a subset of participants who provided detailed information on everything they consumed.
We found that intake estimates lined up closely. This indicated that the questionnaire captured ultra-processed food intake reasonably well.
Participants were followed for cancer incidence for more than 20 years, and more than 10,000 bowel cancer cases were diagnosed.

We used statistical models to estimate associations between ultra-processed food intake and bowel cancer incidence. We accounted for demographic, lifestyle and health-related factors, including physical activity, smoking and drinking alcohol.
We also estimated associations for key dietary factors (dairy, wholegrain, meat) from ultra-processed and non-ultra-processed sources as well as Nova-defined ultra-processed food subgroups.
higher intake of reconstituted meat products, such as hotdogs, was associated with higher bowel cancer incidence
higher intakes of frozen desserts and milk products, such as fruit yoghurts, were associated with lower bowel cancer incidence
higher intakes of breakfast cereals and bread were also associated with lower incidence of bowel cancer
replacing 10% of ultra-processed food intake with the equivalent weight of minimally processed foods was linked to a 2% reduction in the incidence of bowel cancer.
As with any questionnaire-based study, caution is required in interpreting results. Also, our study only found associations, and cannot establish cause and effect.

Still, our findings suggest we should be cautious about drawing conclusions about ultra-processed food as a whole group. The type of ultra-processed food you eat may also be important, when it comes to bowel cancer risk.
Overall, our findings support current dietary guidance for bowel cancer prevention.

That means eating plenty of fruit, vegetables, wholegrains and other fibre-rich foods, as well as limiting intake of red and processed meats (such as hotdogs and cured meats). Limiting alcohol intake is also advised.
