articles.title: Earth’s oldest evidence of life is written in stone – but it’s at risk of disappearing
articles.author: Heidi Jane Allen, Paleontologist, The University of Melbourne
paras: Today, our planet is teeming with life, but it has not always looked the same. Long before forests reached skyward, animals walked on land, and the rise and fall of dinosaurs, our planet was shaped by a much smaller, more unassuming form of life. And we can still find traces of it today.
These ancient fossils, the earliest visible evidence of life on Earth, are known as microbialites.

Western Australia contains an extraordinary record of microbialites: from the oldest known examples, preserved in rocks almost 3.5 billion years old in the Pilbara, to living examples in the UNESCO World Heritage area of Shark Bay.

Our review of 50 years of microbialite research in Western Australia, published today in the journal Alcheringa, summarises what this archive can tell us about the evolution and resilience of life on Earth.

Despite a fossil record that spans billions of years, microbialites are surprisingly fragile. Fossil sites remain vulnerable to over-collection and degradation, while living microbialites are facing growing pressures.

At sites such as Lake Clifton and Shark Bay, some events may have already caused irreparable damage. One such example was in May 2024, when dozens of aurora chasers trampled 2,000-year-old thrombolites in a restricted area at Lake Clifton.
Earth’s oldest evidence of life
Microbialites are mounded structures that come in many shapes and sizes. They form when communities of microbes either precipitate minerals, or trap and bind sediment.
Types of microbialites can be characterised by their internal structure. Stromatolites are the best known, and have distinctive layers. Thrombolites, by contrast, have a clotted texture.

The microbialite record can tell us a great deal about life on Earth. It gives us clues about where some of the earliest life lived, where we might look for life beyond Earth, and how our atmosphere became oxygen rich, paving the way for more complex life to follow.

Modern sites are particularly important because they help us better understand processes that formed microbialites in the ancient rock record. Living microbialites from Shark Bay have even been described as a “Rosetta Stone” for understanding their fossil counterparts.

Microbialites also preserve evidence of how life responded to environmental upheaval in the past. Western Australia’s microbialite record spans at least one, and potentially two, of Earth’s five major mass extinctions.

This deep-time record suggests microbialites may act as early indicators of ecological stress. Evidence suggests that the sudden increase of microbialites often preceded or coincided with major ecological disruption and mass extinction in the past.
Yet our review highlights several significant knowledge gaps.

Scientists are still debating how to distinguish structures built by life from those produced by non-biological processes. We also cannot always say with certainty what environments ancient microbialites formed in.
There is further uncertainty about what controls the shape and structure (morphology) of microbialites. We also don’t fully know how closely modern examples reflect fossil forms.

Why the internal structure of thrombolites is clotted rather than layered, as in stromatolites, remains a conundrum. So does how far back they extend in the geological record. Western Australia may contain some of the oldest known thrombolites, but these examples have not yet been documented in detail.

In short, Earth’s oldest biological record is not a finished story, although the gaps are slowly being filled. Preserving the evidence, both living and fossil, is essential if future scientists are to answer questions we don’t have answers for yet, or perhaps even to ask questions we have not yet thought to ask.
An ancient archive at risk
Despite their geological longevity and seemingly unchanging nature, microbialites are surprisingly fragile. Their rock-like appearance can make this difficult to appreciate.
Living microbialites can be highly sensitive to environmental disturbance. Their extremely slow growth rates mean physical damage can take decades or centuries to repair, if at all.
Many modern microbialite sites face growing pressures from changes in water quality, climate change and increasing visitation.

Fossil microbialites are also vulnerable. Across Western Australia, tourism, inappropriate collecting and even scientific sampling can damage or diminish these irreplaceable sites. As geological features, their protection falls under geoheritage.

Yet geoheritage remains poorly recognised and under resourced in Australia at both the federal and state levels. The 2021 Australian State of the Environment report concluded that “the overall outlook for geoheritage is poor” due to the lack of national frameworks, focus and resourcing for this area of heritage. Unfortunately, little has changed.

Today, we face an unprecedented and accelerating loss of biodiversity. The microbialite archive offers a deep-time perspective on how ecosystems respond to environmental change, ecological disruption and changing conditions. How far these insights can inform our understanding of the challenges facing life today remains an open question.

Just as important is whether the archives themselves, both living and fossil, will remain intact and accessible for future generations to investigate not only the questions we are asking today, but those we have yet to conceive.

Heidi Jane Allen receives funding from the Commonwealth through an Australian Government Research Training Program Scholarship. She was affiliated with the Geological Survey of Western Australia while undertaking this research.

articles.title: In Alberta, far-right populism fuelled by conspiracy theories and alienation drive bid to separate from Canada
articles.author: Gemma Ware, Head of Audio, The Conversation UK, The Conversation
paras: In the western Canadian province of Alberta, a political battle is playing out on people’s front lawns. Separatists are flying the royal blue Alberta flag, others the red and white maple leaf of Canada to show their support for a united Canada.

It’s all because a populist right-wing political movement wants Alberta to break away from the rest of the country. On October 19, Albertans will vote on whether to have a binding referendum on independence.

“Public opinion polls show quite consistently over the last two years that about 70% to 75% of Albertans want to remain in Canada,” explains Jared Wesley, a professor of political science at the University of Alberta to The Conversation Weekly podcast. “So there’s a lot of confusion around the process and why we’re holding this vote in the first place.”

Separatist sentiment is driven in part by a longstanding sense of western alienation from eastern Canada, fuelled by grievances that the province puts more into the federal budget than it gets back. But the current wave of separatism in Alberta also has links to protests against Covid vaccine mandates and conspiracy theories. While most separatists want Alberta to become its own country, some even want the province to be the 51st US state.

Donald Trump’s aggressive trade war with Canada and his attacks on Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney loom large over the poll. Some Albertans who may otherwise have voted in favour of independence to send a message to Ottawa, Wesley says, “are really withholding that support because they worry about what message that sends to the United States.”

The referendum was called by the Alberta premier, Danielle Smith, leader of the province’s United Conservative Party. Despite her support for Alberta remaining in Canada, Smith faced pressure from separatists within her party to hold a referendum. Wesley says Smith’s decision bears similarities with the decision taken by then UK prime minister David Cameron to hold the 2016 Brexit referendum on leaving the European Union:

“More or less, David Cameron called the bluff of his internal Brexiteers that were putting pressure on him, and called a nationwide referendum thinking that he would win it. A lot of the same pressures are at play for Danielle Smith.”

There are ten questions on the ballot, ranging from whether to introduce stricter rules on access to public services for immigrants, to proposals for judicial and constitutional reform. The final question reads:

“Should Alberta remain a province of Canada, or should the government of Alberta commence the legal process required under the Canadian Constitution to hold a binding provincial referendum on whether or not Alberta should separate from Canada?”
Wesley says turnout will be key to how the referendum plays out:
“Very few polls show a reasonable prospect for this first referendum passing. However, in a low turnout situation, the distance between remain and continue the conversation … narrows considerably.”

articles.title: Is the US limiting Starlink in Ukraine? The consequences could be catastrophic
articles.author: Anthony King, Professor of War Studies, Director of the Strategy and Security Institute., University of Exeter
paras: The drone has become the signature weapon of the Russo-Ukraine war. On any day in Ukraine, tens of thousands of drones are out hunting the battlefield for targets. These could be individual enemy soldiers or vehicles, or they could be larger targets such as depots, headquarters, bridges or power plants.

Yet, this drone war has been possible only because of a less obvious but equally vital technology. Elon Musk’s SpaceX Starlink system is a secure digital satellite communications network that Ukraine has become fully reliant on.

When Russia mounted its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, Mykhailo Fedorov – then Ukraine’s vice prime minister and minister of digital transformation – urged Musk publicly to provide connectivity. Two days later, 500 Starlink terminals arrived in Ukraine. In February 2022, Musk granted the Ukrainian government and military the use of Starlink, initially for free. By July 2020, Starlink had provided 15,000 terminals.

The Ukrainians have fully admitted their dependence on Musk: “Without Starlink, we would have been losing the war already,” one platoon commander reportedly told the Wall Street Journal in 2022. Starlink allowed the government and the armed forces to communicate securely, at the heart of its vital system of C4ISR (the military term for command, control, communications, computers, intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance).
Without Starlink, the defence of Ukraine would have been very difficult: perhaps impossible.

The cost to Starlink was considerable, though. Musk initally provided 2,000 terminals for free, 300 discounted and waived monthly services for about 5,500 more. Starlink’s total contribution to the Ukraine war effort in 2022 alone was US$80 million (£71 million). Musk provided a vital military capability gratis and eventually on a (discounted) contractual basis.
The strategic and commercial partnership between Starlink and Ukraine has been vital to the war effort for more than four years.

But Ukraine’s dependency on Starlink – or Starshield as the system’s military application is called – has not come without conditions. In September 2022, having repulsed the initial Russian attacks, the Ukrainian armed forces were planning their first assault on the port city of Sevastopol in Crimea, then the home of Russia’s Black Sea fleet. The plan was to sail remotely controlled boats, loaded with explosives to cripple the fleet.

It was a bold plan – the first attempt by the Ukrainian to attack territory which the Russians had held since 2014 and which they considered sovereign. And it was a controversial attack – the Russian ambassador to the US, Anatoly Antonov, had personally warned Musk that attacking Crimea would be a red line, which could lead to nuclear war.

Musk was concerned. He believed that this was potentially escalatory. He advised Fedorov: “Once Russia is fully mobilised, they will destroy all infrastructure throughout Ukraine.” He urged him to avoid a third world war: “Seek peace while you have the upper hand.”

Musk refused a Ukranian request to activate Starshield operations in the region, posting on X that: “If I had agreed to their request, then SpaceX would be explicitly complicit in a major act of war and conflict escalation.”

But following this crisis, relations between Musk and Ukraine’s leadership stabilised. Starshield has continued to play an indispensable role in Ukraine. It has been the digital communications spine of the Ukrainian armed forces and the enabler of all its operations in this war.

Indeed, when the Ukrainians informed him that in 2026 the Russians had acquired some Starlink terminals on the black market and were accessing the system to help them prosecute the war inside Ukraine, he identified the serial numbers of those terminals and disabled them.

Unfortunately, in the past week, Ukrainian armed forces have once again been exposed to the jeopardy of their dependence on Starlink. On the night of October 13-14, without any warning, SpaceX imposed a speed limit of about 160kmph on some Starlink services, meaning this is the maximum speed Ukrainian drones and missiles can travel and remain connected. Starshield terminals mounted on drones have been particularly badly affected. Ukraine’s 7th Rapid Reaction Corps was forced to cancel several missions.

Given the importance of drones to the Ukrainian war effort, the Starlink constraint is very serious. The speed limit has compromised Ukrainian drone fleets operating above the kill zone. It has also undermined Ukrainian air defence against intensifying Russian drone attacks on cities and infrastructure, as 160kmph is too slow for intercepts.

Since strategic bombardments against Ukrainian energy infrastructure have become Russia’s principal means of prosecuting this war and will only intensify into the winter, the Starlink embargo is deeply concerning. It may become critical if it continues.
Unlike September 2022, it appears that this is not a random individual decision by the Starlink boss. It seems to reflect troubling shifts in US policy on Ukraine.

On October 9, the US president, Donald Trump announced a deal with his Russian counterpart, Vladimir Putin, to lift sanctions on Russian diesel and allow it access to global markets. The plan was, he said, to reduce the price of fuel – although how effectively the relatively small amount of Russian diesel will do that is unclear. The high price of diesel is much more to do with the intractable war in Iran.

The following day, Trump called for the removal of Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelensky: “Time for Ukraine to get a new president”, he told reporters. The day after that, the US president announced that an energy ceasefire was in immediate effect and that Russia and Ukraine would stop targeting each other’s energy infrastructure.

Ukraine has not used Starlink to hit Russia’s oil refineries. Starlink does not work in Russia and the Ukraine deep strikes rely on other communications systems. So Ukraine’s strategic bombardments remain technically unaffected by the Starlink embargo.

Musk has put the responsibility for the slowdown in Starshield squarely on the US government, posting on his X social media platform: “Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government. Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS.”

In September 2022, Musk instituted a policy which contradicted US policy on Ukraine – he turned off Starlink against the wishes of the Biden administration. Now, so Musk says, in October 2026, it’s US government which is restricting Starlink. But the result is effectively the same: Ukraine is the victim.
This winter always looked as if it will be hard for Ukraine. It just got harder.

articles.title: Can Ethiopia ever be at peace? Four reasons conflict keeps flaring up
articles.author: Alemayehu Fentaw Weldemariam, Adjunct Professor and Ph.D. Fellow, Center for Constitutional Democracy, Indiana University
paras: Ethiopia has experienced recurrent conflicts for over five decades. This includes a long-running civil war sparked by the overthrow of Emperor Haile Selassie in 1974, renewed fighting in Tigray, and ongoing conflicts in Amhara and Oromia.
The renewed hostilities in Tigray threaten to undo a peace process that had begun with an agreement signed in Pretoria, South Africa, in 2022.
Why has peace been so difficult to sustain in Ethiopia? My research on constitutional design and conflict points to four interconnected explanations:
the foundations of the Ethiopian state remain contested
ceasefires are mistaken for political settlements
armed force continues to be a route to political power
regional rivalries reinforce internal conflicts.

The problem isn’t that Ethiopians of diverse ethnic backgrounds hate one another and can’t live together peacefully. It’s that successive political arrangements have failed to establish widely accepted rules for managing disagreements.
1. The foundations of the state remain contested
Ethiopia’s 1995 constitution emerged from a political transition that followed the overthrow of the military government in 1991. This ended nearly two decades of civil war.

The new leadership sought to address long-standing grievances over ethnic marginalisation and demands for greater autonomy. It restructured the country as a federation largely organised around ethnolinguistic communities. The constitution vested sovereignty in Ethiopia’s nations, nationalities and peoples. It guaranteed their right to self-determination, including secession.
Proponents of federalism regard this right as protection against historical domination. Opponents argue that it entrenches ethnic boundaries and encourages competition over territory and resources.
Ethnic diversity doesn’t inevitably lead to violence. And federalism isn’t inherently destabilising. It was introduced to accommodate competing national claims within a common political order.
But constitutional recognition is not the same as political reconciliation.

The problem arises when a constitution sets out rules for sharing power and governing the country without sufficient agreement among the political groups expected to follow them. Instead of providing a common framework for resolving disputes, those rules become another source of political conflict.
2. Ceasefires are mistaken for political settlements

The 2022 Pretoria agreement was about stopping hostilities, not about resolving their causes. The federal government and the Tigray People’s Liberation Front agreed to end two years of war. Major political questions were left for later negotiation.
Disputed territories, regional administration, political participation and accountability for wartime abuses remain contentious.
Eritrea, a major participant in the 2020-2022 war in Tigray, did not sign the agreement. Eritrean forces are still present in parts of Tigray.

The Tigray People’s Liberation Front itself also became fragmented after the war. Divisions emerged within the leadership. Disagreements over federal relations, political authority and control of military forces developed into a struggle within the movement.

A peace agreement assumes that the parties signing it have authority over their political and military organisations to honour their commitments. But when these organisations fragment, it becomes unclear who can carry out agreements.
The Tigray leadership’s loss of legal party status in 2025 added another obstacle to political reintegration.
These developments have undermined confidence that the transition from armed conflict to constitutional politics would be honoured.

This distinction is fundamental. A cessation of hostilities can save lives immediately. But it cannot, by itself, establish a legitimate regional government, resolve territorial claims or restore trust between former enemies.
3. Armed force is a route to political power

The use of violence to acquire or retain political authority has deep roots in Ethiopia’s modern history. In 1974, the military overthrew the empire-state and established a military regime. This regime was itself overthrown in 1991 by a coalition of rebel forces led by the Ethiopian People’s Revolutionary Democratic Front.

These transitions reinforced a pattern in which political power could be won through armed struggle. When political opponents have little confidence that elections, courts or negotiations can bring change, taking up arms can appear more effective than peaceful political competition.
The continued use of force by both the state and armed groups makes this cycle difficult to break.

Abiy Ahmed became prime minister in 2018 after years of anti-government protests and divisions within the ruling coalition. Two years later, rising political tensions led to war in Tigray. Abiy’s regime has faced accusations of serious rights abuses and a lack of accountability.

This has deepened distrust. It’s made negotiated settlements harder to achieve. Under Abiy, political authority has become increasingly personalised. Military operations and extraordinary security measures have been used to confront political challenges.
Peace needs a political environment where losing an election doesn’t mean exclusion from power or exposure to coercion.
4. Regional rivalries reinforce internal conflicts

Ethiopia’s domestic conflicts are increasingly intersecting with the interests and actions of neighbouring countries. Eritrean forces fought beside Ethiopia’s army in Tigray. They remained in parts of the region after the 2022 peace deal. Now the former allies are adversaries.
There have been accusations of cross-border military intervention. This has renewed concerns that the war in Tigray could develop into a wider conflict.
Ethiopia’s ambitions to secure Red Sea access have further complicated relations with Eritrea and Somalia. Its 2024 agreement with Somaliland provoked a dispute with Mogadishu.

Ethiopia also has strained relations with Egypt over its mega dam in the Nile River. Sudan’s ongoing civil war and rival Saudi Arabia and Emirati relationships across the Red Sea add further pressures.
These external tensions can make domestic troubles harder to contain. Ethiopia has a duty to defend its boundaries and also to respect those of its neighbours.
What would lasting peace require?
These four obstacles to peace reinforce one another:
disagreements over constitutional rules fuel political tensions
armed conflict makes inclusive negotiations more difficult
peace agreements that fail to address underlying grievances leave the door open to renewed violence
competing regional interests complicate efforts to achieve lasting peace.
As a result, Ethiopia’s recurring conflicts cannot be resolved through ceasefires alone.
Lasting peace requires all Ethiopians to agree on how power is shared, and the relationship between the federal government and its regions.

But resolving Ethiopia’s internal divisions will not, on its own, settle tensions with neighbouring countries. That requires diplomacy built on respect for sovereignty, non-interference and peaceful negotiation over interests.
Ethiopia therefore faces two interconnected challenges. First, building a political system that its diverse communities can accept. Second, establishing peaceful relations with its neighbours.
Lasting peace depends on both.

Alemayehu Fentaw Weldemariam does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organisation that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.

articles.title: Young voters fear mass shootings but are divided on gun control
articles.author: Jillian Turanovic, Professor of Sociology, University of Colorado Boulder
paras: An updated version of this article was published on Oct. 16, 2026. Read it here.

Nearly 50 million Americans ages 18 to 29 are eligible to vote in the upcoming midterm elections, and about 60% say they plan to. If they follow through, it would break midterm turnout records for voters under 30.

Gun control is an issue these young voters care about more than the public at large does, and it’s easy to understand why: In their lifetime, mass shootings have been a recurring part of American life.

Directly experiencing a mass shooting is rare, yet some young people have survived two before turning 25. When a gunman opened fire at Brown University in December 2025, at least two students on campus had already experienced a school shooting before they got to college. The same thing happened in April 2025, when students who lived through the 2018 Parkland, Florida, shooting at Marjory Stoneman Douglas High School found themselves caught in another shooting at Florida State University. As one of them put it: “This is America.”

Researchers have called today’s young adults the “massacre generation.” They’re the first group to grow up entirely in the post-9/11, post-Columbine High School shooting era, with routine lockdown drills, heightened security in schools and nonstop media coverage of mass violence.

As criminologists who study the impacts of victimization and gun violence among young people, we wanted to know how growing up with the threat of mass shootings has shaped young adults’ views on gun legislation. In a recent study, we surveyed nearly 1,700 young adults, ages 18 to 29, across the country to find out. We found that fear of mass shootings pulls this generation apart along political and gender lines: It pushes some toward wanting stricter gun laws and others in the opposite direction.
A debate that repeats after every shooting

Mass shootings account for about 1% of gun deaths in the U.S. Still, they profoundly shape how safe millions of Americans feel. In a 2019 survey by the American Psychological Association, nearly 80% of Americans said the possibility of a mass shooting stressed them out, and a third said they avoided certain places because of it. The fear has become so common that clinicians now have screening tools to assess and treat people with anxiety over mass violence.

Young adults have also grown up watching the same heated gun debates play out after every tragedy. Gun control advocates call for stricter firearm restrictions to prevent the next mass shooting, whereas gun rights advocates push back with the “good guy with a gun” argument, a phrase made popular by the National Rifle Association. Supporters of the latter view say more armed citizens are needed to stop active shooters, so more people should be able to buy and carry guns with fewer restrictions, such as carrying in public without a permit or on college campuses.

Researchers have known for a long time that more guns don’t necessarily mean less violence. A 2021 study found that mass shootings were more common in states with higher rates of gun ownership, and gun homicides were more common in states with looser concealed carry laws. Yet even after decades of mass shootings, federal gun policy has barely budged. Even where individual states and local governments have passed assault weapons bans, including Connecticut and Cook County, Illinois, they’ve faced Second Amendment challenges that are now before the Supreme Court.

Young people have become some of the loudest voices in this debate, most notably through March for Our Lives – an organization started by Parkland survivors that focuses on ending gun violence – and other youth-led groups across the country. And because pro-gun views tend to be more common among older Americans, many political observers assume stricter gun laws will follow as young people gain voting power.

This fall, voters will choose members of Congress and state lawmakers who can shape gun laws, and in a few states they’ll weigh in on gun policy directly. In Massachusetts, voters will decide whether to keep or repeal a 2024 law that, among other things, requires gun owners to register their firearms with the state, expands safety training for people applying for a gun license and broadens the state’s ban on assault-style weapons. In Arkansas, they’ll decide whether to change the state constitution to more strongly protect gun rights, including the right to own ammunition and gun parts. If young adults turn out in record numbers, their views could help determine outcomes like these.

So where do young adults stand? We’ve found that a shared fear of mass shootings does not necessarily lead to shared views on guns. Our survey asked young adults to rate on a scale from 1 to 3 – from “not at all” to “a lot” – how much they fear that they or someone they love will become a victim of a mass shooting. More than 60% reported moderate or high levels of fear, including about 17% who fell in the high-fear range.

In general, about two-thirds of young adults said people should need a permit to carry a gun in public and that guns shouldn’t be allowed on college campuses. About 6 in 10 disagreed that owning more guns makes people safer, and a similar share disagreed that gun control laws are unconstitutional.

We found that young adults who worried more about mass shootings tended to be more supportive of gun control. But this pattern didn’t hold for young men, Republicans or those who were politically conservative. For these groups, the opposite was true: The more they feared mass shootings, the less they supported gun restrictions. Young adults are divided on gun control, and those divisions are sharpest when fear runs high.

In the coming years, the massacre generation is on track to become part of the largest voting bloc in the country. Most young adults share a fear of mass shootings, but they disagree on what to do about them. And with each new mass shooting, that divide may only deepen.

articles.title: Cities are sinking – but citywide averages hide the real problem
articles.author: Emma Colven, Senior Lecturer in Environment and Society, King's College London
paras: Cities worldwide are sinking at alarming rates, but that doesn’t mean the ground is sinking at the same rate everywhere. Some neighbourhoods may be far more affected than others close by, with serious consequences for their residents.

Land subsidence – the gradual sinking of the ground surface – is a global urban problem. Rapid development often drives excessive groundwater extraction, which can cause underground sediments to compact and the land above to sink. The risk of flooding is exacerbated by rising sea levels and more intense rainfall associated with climate change.
One recent study estimated that about 71% of the global coastal population lives in subsiding regions, many of which are densely populated and already threatened by sea-level rise.

Advances in satellite monitoring now allow researchers to measure subsidence across cities at fine spatial scales. In a new study in Nature Cities a team of Chinese scientists used nine years of these satellite images to assess 465 large cities worldwide. They found cities in Asia are subsiding fastest, and that cities in developing countries are generally sinking faster than those in wealthier countries.
But citywide patterns can conceal big differences within individual cities, with important implications for where flood protection is most needed.
Jakarta – among the world’s fastest sinking cities

We have become very aware of this in our own research in the Indonesian capital Jakarta. Now the world’s most populous city, Jakarta has for many years been the poster child for sinking cities. Significant areas already lie below sea level and continued subsidence could put more of the city below it. Some areas in Jakarta are sinking more rapidly than others: the city’s northern coastal area, for instance, sinks up to 7cm a year according to our model for 2016-24.

As a low-lying delta city in the tropics, crossed by 13 rivers, Jakarta is already vulnerable to floods from both rivers and tides. Land subsidence makes these floods more frequent and severe. In coastal northern areas such as Muara Angke, where informal settlements are common, flooding can occur every other day. This affects some of the city’s most vulnerable communities.
Land subsidence is a planning problem

To protect the city, Jakarta has constructed a network of seawalls, water gates, polder systems, dykes, and pumping stations. Something similar is needed in many other subsiding coastal cities on Java, the world’s most populated island, and there are now plans to construct a giant sea wall across much of northern Java.
Yet flood defences alone won’t be able to cope and protect Jakarta or other Javanese cities from flooding without changes to the overall planning system.

Land subsidence had not been fully integrated into Jakarta’s flood management planning until recently. Groundwater extraction regulations were introduced in 2021 and implemented in 2023, despite land subsidence being discussed for more than three decades.

A core problem remains the lack of a reliable piped water supply, making it desirable for residential and large commercial buildings to extract their own groundwater. Enforcement has improved but remains challenging: groundwater is notoriously difficult to manage as it is a hidden or “fugitive” resource.

Fortunately, land subsidence from excessive groundwater extraction can be reversed. When groundwater is replenished, the land surface may rise again. That being said, even immediately stopping groundwater extraction would not halt sinking abruptly.
Long-term adaptive management is urgently needed, supported by a comprehensive policy framework that combines groundwater regulation, extraction control, and overall water supply management.

Injecting water into the ground to replenish the aquifer has proven effective in managing subsidence in places such as Las Vegas and Shanghai. But the same approach is not straightforward in Jakarta, where land subsidence is driven by a combination of factors, including water loss deep below ground. Addressing this is technically complex and expensive, making regulation and piped water essential to tackling the problem.

Subsidence may be a global problem, but it is driven by locally specific factors and can only be addressed with an understanding of local patterns. This is because the causes and impacts of land subsidence are shaped by urban development, water management, and all the other policies and decisions in the making of the city.

As cities worldwide continue to sink, we need to continually examine these changes at the local scale. Averages across a whole city can tell us how big the problem is, but knowing where the land is sinking fastest – and who lives there – is essential to deciding how best to respond.

articles.title: ‘Sodcit’ – after battlefield setbacks, Russia returns to destroying Ukraine’s morale
articles.author: Tracey German, Professor of Conflict and Security, King's College London
paras: Ukrainian President Volodymr Zelensky recently told journalists that the Russian president, Vladimir Putin, has instructed his military commanders to abandon the rules of war that protect civilian targets. “He said there are no rules now,” Zelensky said – reporting that this information had been picked up by intelligence intercepts of Russian communications.

That Putin’s commanders took him at his word is apparent from a sharp increase in strikes on civilian targets. Over the past month there has been an intensification of Russian strikes on Kyiv and other Ukrainian cities. A UN report on October 9 reported that: “On 27 September alone, alerts lasted 19 hours. Strikes on bridges, educational institutions and energy infrastructure have intensified, causing widespread blackouts and water supply disruptions.”

On October 11, the US president, Donald Trump, announced an “energy ceasefire” which he said had been agreed to by both Russia and Ukraine. But both sides have denied this. While Zelensky has said Ukraine will halt its successful campaign of strikes against Russian oil refineries if Russia stops targeting its power plants, Russia responded the same day with a series of attacks on Ukrainian power facilities.

Other critical infrastructure targeted by Russian strikes has included data centres and internet providers in Kyiv and other big cities. Russia has also been targeting transport and logistics hubs, rail stations and bridges over the Dnipro river in Kyiv.
All of these are severely disruptive to civilian life. In the case of Kyiv’s bridges, their destruction has the potential to literally bring the city to a standstill.

Distinguishing between civilian targets and military objectives is a fundamental principle of international humanitarian law on the conduct of war. This expressly prohibits attacks against civilians and civilian objects.

The rule is codified in Article 48 of the Geneva Convention, to which Russia is a signatory. The article states that all parties to a conflict “shall at all times distinguish between the civilian population and combatants and between civilian objects and military objectives and […] shall direct their operations only against military objectives”.
Russian military regulations on international humanitarian law nominally endorse distinction and proportionality. Russia is also a party to the Geneva Conventions.

But Russian practice has often diverged from its formal legal commitments. During military operations in Chechnya, Syria and Ukraine, the Russian armed forces engaged in patterns of behaviour that directly violated these principles. Russian forces fighting in Chechnya relied heavily on the use of massive firepower and the indiscriminate use of force.

The Russian siege of the Chechen capital Grozny, in 1999 and 2000, devastated the city, prompting the UN to label it “the most destroyed city on Earth” . Russian operations in Syria echoed this approach. Its military conducted intense bombing raids and indiscriminate airstrikes against residential areas and civilian infrastructure such as schools, hospitals and markets.

Attacking critical non-military targets has been part of the way Russia has waged war for many years. Soviet military theorist Aleksandr Svechin distinguished between two different strategies of warfare. A strategy of destruction aims to destroy enemy armed forces quickly with a knock-out blow in the field. A strategy of exhaustion, on the other hand, depends on degrading an enemy’s economic, material and moral resources over time. These ideas remain influential.

Svechin’s strategy of exhaustion is often summed up by military theorists with the acronym Sodcit. Spelled out in full, this stands for “strategic operations to destroy critical infrastructure”. It’s a key element of Russia’s way of waging war.

But Sodcit isn’t about indiscriminate attacks on civilian targets. The idea is to “inflict sufficient material and psychological ‘deterrent damage’ to reduce the adversary’s capacity and, above all, willingness to continue or escalate the war”.

It’s interesting to note, though, that when reporting Russian strikes on Ukraine, the state news agency, Tass – a Kremlin mouthpiece – aims to establish these are “dual-use targets”. In other words, they can also be used for military purposes. So a Nova Post logistic hub, where people’s parcels and other mail are sorted, was, Tass claimed, “used to store dual-use cargo designated for supplies to the Ukrainian army”.
But it’s much harder to justify bombing apartment blocks and cities’ electricity installations in military terms.

So as winter approaches, destroying Ukraine’s energy networks and leaving people without heating, power or water, aims to destroy morale. And when civilian infrastructure is targeted, civilians also die. The UN human rights monitoring mission in Ukraine (HRMMU) has reported that civilian casualties in the first eight months of 2026 were higher than the whole of 2025. This is also calculated to destroy morale.

Putin’s “new strategy” of attacking civilians and the things that enable them to go about their lives is nothing new. But it seems clear that with winter approaching, and in light of recent Ukrainian success on the front lines, Russia will redouble its attacks on Ukraine’s home front.
Tracey German receives funding from the Russia Strategic Initiative (RSI).

articles.title: Norway’s Telenor telecom faces lawsuit for giving user data to Myanmar junta
articles.author: Mong Palatino
paras: The state-owned company is accused of abetting crimes against humanity
Originally published on Global Voices
Telenor telecom operated in Myanmar from 2014 to 2022. Photo by Bjoertvedt. Source: Wikipedia. CC BY-SA 4.0

This post is part of Global Voices’ October 2026 Spotlight series, “Big Tech and Authoritarianism.” In this Spotlight, we explore how Big Tech facilitates and hinders authoritarian governments and practices, and how these choices influence the Global South. You can support this coverage by donating here.
The Norway-based multinational telecom company Telenor is facing charges for its role in turning over sensitive customer data to the military government of Myanmar.
If successful, the case would be the first ever to hold a telecom company accountable for failing to protect user data from being misused by an authoritarian regime.

Telenor operated in Myanmar from 2014 to 2022 with 18 million subscribers. After the February 2021 coup, Telenor faced pressure after the junta demanded compliance with its surveillance and content blocking directives. Telenor decided to leave Myanmar, but civil society groups raised strong objections that its local operations would be sold to a company with links to the junta.

In December 2024, activist group Justice For Myanmar filed a complaint against Telenor in Norway for breach of the Sanctions Act. Norway rejected it, but the complaint was refiled in October 2025 with an additional charge of aiding and abetting crimes against humanity.

The Norwegian state has a 54-percent stake in Telenor. In December 2025, the Norwegian Parliament initiated an investigation into the operations of Telenor in Myanmar. The leader of the disciplinary committee of the Parliament said: “We must uncover how a state-owned company could cooperate with a brutal military regime (by handing over) customer information about the opposition [in Myanmar].”

In April 2026, a civil class action lawsuit was filed against Telenor in Norway by Myanmar citizens for sharing their sensitive personal data with the junta. The complaint alleged that Telenor shared at least 1,253 phone numbers with the regime. The data also included call logs and location data, names, addresses, ID numbers, Facebook, and bank accounts linked to mobile numbers.

Among the complainants is Tha Zin, the widow of rapper and lawmaker Phyo Zeya Thaw, who was arrested based on a trumped-up charge, convicted, and later executed by the junta. Tha Zin said her husband was arrested right after his account information was accessed by the junta.

I lost my husband. It is not just a wife losing her husband. It is also a loss to the movement. It is also a loss to democracy because my husband was committed to democracy and a youth leader. Losing him means a loss to the country.
Lawyer Jan Magne Langseth summed up the content of the complaint.

Telenor ASA in Norway clearly contributed to the practice of handing over user data, despite the inherent risks for its customers in Myanmar. We have evidence of cases where the team at HQ expressly recommended the data to be handed over.
In September 2026, Norway’s National Criminal Investigation Service and the interior security service searched the office of Telenor related to the charges filed against the company.
Justice for Myanmar spokesperson Yadanar Maung welcomed the decision of Norway authorities to investigate Telenor.

Telenor’s transfer of spyware to a military-linked company and sharing of sensitive data with the military junta was extensively documented We hope this will finally lead to accountability for the harms Telenor has caused Myanmar people through its conduct and its dangerous divestment.
In several statements sent to the media, Telenor said it is cooperating with authorities with regard to the ongoing investigation. It added that it needed to defend its employees in Myanmar.

In Myanmar, refusing requests from the military authorities could, in the worst case, have led to imprisonment, torture or the death penalty. Telenor Myanmar had no real options. We could not play Russian roulette with the lives of our employees.
Telenor media relations director David Fidjeland reiterated the same point.

Our employees risked imprisonment, torture or the death penalty if the military authorities’ orders were not complied with. We found that we had no real choice and that we could not put our employees’ lives at risk.
Telenor acknowledged the brutality of the junta, but it asserted that the welfare of its employees should not be endangered.

Telenor acknowledges that human rights due diligence must consider all rights-holders. However, when faced with the brutal force of the military, Telenor maintains that an employer cannot give instructions that put employees’ lives at direct risk.
Civil society groups said the investigation is a step forward in fighting impunity. Civicus said companies should not enable human rights abuses.

The Telenor case has the potential to challenge impunity. It should refocus the minds of democratic states and companies headquartered in them, offering a warning that they can be exposed for complicity in the junta’s atrocities. It should give fresh impetus to civil society’s efforts to hold states and companies to account.

Faiz Naeem, Asia Pacific policy analyst at Access Now, added that Telenor’s case is a reminder for companies that their obligation to users does not end when leaving a country under an autocratic regime.

The decision to investigate Telenor for crimes against humanity should be a wake-up call for every technology and telecom company operating in a high-risk environment: leaving a market does not mean leaving your human rights responsibilities behind.
The civil class action lawsuit is seeking damages of EUR 9,000 (roughly USD 10,500) per customer.

articles.title: In Kyrgyzstan, persons with disabilities are collecting proof of physical barriers to hold the government accountable
articles.author: Nurbek Bekmurzaev
paras: Physical barriers are being exposed by those who are affected the most
Originally published on Global Voices
Participants of the Oasis Data Lab workshop in Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan. Image by the public fund Oasis. Used with permission.

This interview is part of a series of spotlights on the work of some of the grantees of the Digital Spark granting scheme, as part of the Regional Support Mechanism EECA project, implemented by the Metamorphosis Foundation and TechSoup, in partnership with CIVICUS and under the Digital Democracy Initiative (DDI) that covers the Global South. It is being published on Global Voices as part of a content-sharing agreement.

Kyrgyzstan’s progress in creating an inclusive and accessible environment for people with disabilities remains limited after seven years of ratifying the United Nations (UN) Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities in 2019.

Despite a legal responsibility to undertake measures that would remove legal and physical barriers and help people with disabilities lead independent social and economic lives, the government has not prioritized this commitment at the level requested by the country’s disabled community.

In such circumstances, holding the government accountable requires proof of how much physical infrastructure remains inaccessible for the more than 218,000 people with disabilities in the country — about three percent of the population.

One of the organizations leading this effort in Kyrgyzstan is the public fund “Oasis”, which is documenting the level of physical inaccessibility in the capital, Bishkek, with the help of people with disabilities who are auditing objects through their real-life experiences. Global Voices conducted a written interview with Oasis to learn about this work, which is being carried out under the Digital Sparks project. The interview has been edited for clarity and brevity.
Global Voices (GV): Please tell us about your organization and why you chose to get involved with the Digital Sparks project.

Oasis (O): Founded in 2003, Oasis is a Kyrgyz civil society organization working to build inclusive communities where everyone can participate and reach their full potential. We joined the project because we know that it is not possible to build an inclusive city without listening to the people navigating its barriers every day. In Bishkek, we saw accessibility discussed through policies and assumptions, while lived experiences remained largely invisible. We wanted to change that to make exclusion visible, measurable, and impossible to overlook with the help of data. Digital Sparks helped us build the Oasis Data Lab, bringing together citizen-generated data, digital mapping, storytelling, and advocacy. Our goal was not simply to create a map, but to build a bridge between lived experience and public decision-making, turning everyday barriers into evidence for change.
GV: What issue/challenge in your community prompted you to undertake this project?

O: The project grew from a practical problem: people with disabilities face barriers across Bishkek, but these barriers were not being systematically documented. Public transport, entrances, ramps, toilets, signage, and other parts of the urban environment can make everyday participation difficult. Yet without reliable and regularly updated data, these problems remain easy to overlook. Kyrgyzstan ratified the UN Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities in 2019, but there is still a gap between formal commitments and everyday accessibility. Previous assessments were limited and did not create a living public record that could be used to monitor progress. We therefore started from a simple principle: before accessibility can be improved, it has to be measured. And the people who experience these barriers every day should be directly involved in producing that evidence.
GV: What are the key changes/activities that your organization implemented during your participation in the project?

O: Through Digital Sparks, we developed Oasis Data Lab into a more structured space for digital civic participation. We brought together more than 30 young people, including people with physical disabilities, blind and low-vision participants, deaf participants, social activists, and urban experts. We organized workshops on disability rights, inclusivity, digital advocacy, data collection, mapping, and storytelling. A major practical change was integrating UrbanEyes into our work. Through the application, participants can assess buildings using geolocation, photographs, questionnaires, and standardized accessibility indicators. The web platform then visualizes this information through an interactive map, filters, heat maps, and accessibility indices. Most importantly, the project moved us from collecting individual complaints toward creating structured, comparable civic data that can support advocacy, dialogue with authorities, and evidence-based urban planning.
GV: How did your participation in the project impact your organization’s beneficiaries and the community that you serve? Please provide examples.

O: One of the biggest impacts has been the shift in how participants are positioned: not simply as beneficiaries, but as researchers, digital monitors, and civic actors. Participants have already assessed 350 buildings across Bishkek and transformed their observations into geo-referenced data for the city’s accessibility map. The results show the scale of the problem clearly: 60.3 percent of assessed buildings had a ramp-related barrier, either because there was no ramp or because the existing ramp was difficult or unsuitable to use. The project also allows participants to compare accessibility across districts and types of buildings, rather than relying only on individual complaints. Just as importantly, participants are learning to communicate findings through digital storytelling and advocacy. Their lived experience is becoming structured evidence that can be presented directly to decision-makers and used to argue for concrete improvements.
GV: How has your own knowledge, awareness, and experience with digital democracy and civic space changed, thanks to your participation in the project?

O: The project changed our understanding of digital democracy. We previously saw digital tools mainly as instruments for research, communication, and advocacy. Digital Sparks helped us understand their deeper democratic potential: digital democracy can change not only how information is shared, but who gets to produce it, whose voices are visible, and who participates in decision-making. Participatory mapping showed that technology can shift evidence production closer to communities themselves. People can document the barriers they experience, make them visible, and use this evidence to demand change. We also learned that digital democracy must be accessible, safe, and rights-based. More importantly, we realized that as society becomes increasingly digital, traditional forms of participation alone are no longer enough. Digital democracy offers an opportunity to make civic participation more inclusive, responsive, and effective.
GV: What are the most valuable lessons and experiences you are taking away from this project?

O: Our most valuable lesson is that “Nothing About Us Without Us” should apply not only to policymaking, but also to the evidence on which policy is based. Lived experience can reveal things that a conventional audit may miss. A checklist may show that a building has a ramp, while a wheelchair user can show that the ramp is too steep, slippery, too narrow, lacks handrails, or still does not allow independent access. We also learned that data must remain dynamic. Accessibility cannot be measured once and considered solved; information needs to be updated and connected to advocacy. Finally, data alone does not create change. Its value comes from combining reliable evidence with storytelling, community leadership, public communication, and structured dialogue with institutions. That combination is what turns information into civic power.
GV: What comes next? How will you apply the learning and digital capacity you have built in your future work and within your community?

O: Our next step is to make Oasis Data Lab a long-term civic innovation and evidence hub rather than a one-time project. We plan to continue developing the UrbanEyes app and Bishkek’s Accessibility Map, regularly updating the data and using it to identify priority areas and support public accountability. We also intend to use the findings in dialogue with Bishkek’s Mayor’s Office, the Ministry of Labour, Social Protection and Migration, civil society, businesses, and other stakeholders. The data can help identify areas requiring urgent improvement and support more informed infrastructure planning and budgeting. Participants will be encouraged to continue contributing data, producing digital stories, and sharing their skills with other young advocates. In the longer term, we want to adapt this model to other regions, especially rural ones.

articles.title: Yemen’s Houthis are bringing their war to Saudi Arabia – and reframing the narrative of being an Iranian proxy
articles.author: Laurent Bonnefoy, CNRS research fellow, Center for International Studies, Sciences Po
paras: A deadly Houthi attack on Riyadh’s international airport has highlighted how the Yemeni group is reframing its perceived “Iran proxy” role and shifting its regional focus to its ongoing battle against Saudi Arabia. The Oct. 10 strike, in which 13 people were killed and hundreds injured, was the most violent episode on Saudi Arabian soil since the beginning of the war in Iran in February.
It was followed by further – albeit less deadly – missile barrages in the days since. The violence, moreover, comes just as the kingdom is hosting a major conference for oil producers.

As a longtime analyst of Yemeni politics, I see the latest attacks as another illustration of both the expanding regional stalemate across the Middle East and the need to understand how Yemen’s decade-long war is having effects far beyond its territory.

The Houthi movement first emerged as a militarized political actor in Yemen in 2004 and has been locked in a multiyear civil war against the internationally recognized, Saudi-backed central government. Currently, the Houthis control about a third of the territory and two-thirds of the population. They are undoubtedly Yemen’s most powerful armed force, despite lacking access to warplanes, and have developed an arsenal of long-range missiles and drones.
All along, the Houthis have frequently been portrayed by their adversaries and many external observers as a proxy for Iran, the chief regional rival to Saudi Arabia.

It’s true that the movement has long been broadly aligned with Tehran and frequently shared regional objections, even if the relationship is complex and varied. At the same time, the evolution of the Houthi movement remains intimately connected to Yemen’s domestic political context and to a historical feud specific to the country – something I and many other scholars have researched.

What is particularly significant in the current context of an escalating fight with Saudi Arabia, however, is the way in which the Houthi leadership has sought to reframe its military engagement over the course of 2026 so that it does not appear to be directed by Iran.
This shift is analytically important because it reveals how Houthi leaders understand the political effectiveness of particular narratives and how they seek to legitimize their actions.

When the United States and Israel launched their attack on Iran on Feb. 28, many observers expected the Houthis to enter the conflict swiftly. Their previous intervention in the Red Sea – between November 2023 and May 2025 – in support of Palestinians after Israel’s war in Gaza had, to some extent, provided a blueprint for disrupting maritime traffic through the Strait of Hormuz.

The symbolic returns of their earlier campaign had been considerable. On the one hand, it demonstrated the Houthis’ willingness to act in support of Gaza at a time when many Arab governments were widely perceived as turning their backs on the plight of Palestinians. It also revealed the movement’s capacity to disrupt global supply chains and affect international trade far beyond Yemen.

But the Houthis remained on the sidelines for several months after the initial U.S.-Israeli strikes on Iran. Their leaders appeared to disregard reports that Iranian decision-makers had called on them, in July 2026, to close the Strait of Bab el-Mandeb to maritime traffic.

Assuming that the Houthis would automatically act at Tehran’s command reflected a misreading of Yemeni history and of the identity markers that shape the movement’s political legitimacy. Acting in support of Palestinians could be framed for a domestic and regional audience as an expression of Arab solidarity. But acting on behalf of Iran, a non-Arab Persian country composed almost entirely of Twelver Shia Muslims, was considerably more difficult to rationalize in Arab Yemen where Twelver Shia Muslims are absent and Sunnis are the majority.
The Houthis’ reentry into the regional conflict in August took place alongside a shift in their political narrative, which increasingly centered on their long-standing adversary, Saudi Arabia.

Although the strategic consequences of their actions may ultimately benefit Iran in its own regional and international conflicts, the Houthis see their military campaign against Saudi Arabia chiefly as an act of national defense.
An earlier airport bombing

During the summer of 2026, an important episode went largely unnoticed in the Western media: the Houthis’ attempt to establish the reopening of Sanaa International Airport through the surprise departure of a Tehran-bound flight and its subsequent return.

The airport, located in the Houthi-controlled capital, had been closed since late 2024 following Israeli strikes. Its continued closure meant that access to and exit from Houthi-controlled territory remained subject to restrictions imposed by the movement’s adversaries. These included the authorities controlling Aden, the interim capital of the internationally recognized government.

From the Houthis’ perspective, their sovereignty consequently remained incomplete. The airport’s closure not only restricted civilian movement but also limited their ability to send supporters abroad for training and potentially to receive military equipment. On July 13, the Saudi military’s subsequent bombing of the Sanaa runway, as the incoming aircraft from Tehran approached, provided the movement an opportunity to reignite its confrontation with Riyadh.

After more than three years of a de facto ceasefire and difficult negotiations, Riyadh appeared, as in its dealings with Iran, increasingly eager to extricate itself from the region’s protracted conflicts. Sensing an opening, the Houthi leadership responded by invoking a logic of tit-for-tat retaliation.

The Houthis’ tactics today are a kind of mirror to the 2015 launch of a Saudi-led bombing campaign and blockade of the Houthi-controlled parts of Yemen that has led to years of protracted civil war. The Houthis now claim the right to impose reciprocal restrictions on Saudi Arabia, particularly by targeting its ports and oil-exporting infrastructure.

The Houthis’ new tactic serves two purposes. First, it allows the Houthis to redirect responsibility for the economic and humanitarian crisis in and around Sanaa toward the Saudi-enforced blockade rather than their own governance failures, mismanagement and corruption. Second, it provides a rationale for escalating the conflict across the region.

Previously, the Houthi military leadership had halted attacks on Israeli-linked shipping in the Red Sea following the formal Gaza ceasefire of October 2025, despite having repeatedly come under bombardment. It had likewise suspended attacks on American vessels following an agreement with the Trump administration in May 2025.

These decisions demonstrated a degree of pragmatism beneath the movement’s inflammatory rhetoric. That pragmatism appeared to persist even as the Houthis resumed their regional military engagement, with American diplomats reportedly meeting Houthi representatives in Oman in September 2026.

With Saudi Arabia, however, the Houthis felt less compunction. Riyadh was already facing repeated barrages of Iran missiles as a consequences of its alliance with the U.S. and facing an energy export squeeze. So with the Saudi airport incident, the Houthi leadership feels it has trapped Saudi Arabia, with consequences extending to the global economy.

This retaliatory strategy was bolstered by successful Houthi moves in early September to establish a degree of control over the Strait of Bab el-Mandeb, one of the world’s most important maritime choke points. That gave the Houthis leverage over shipping crucial for Saudi Arabia in the Red Sea.
Drones and ballistic missiles, as the attacks on the Riyadh airport illustrate, also give the movement the capacity to strike targets across much of Saudi Arabia.
The targeting of civilian infrastructure in Saudi Arabia, particularly airports, illustrates the retaliatory logic the Houthis have invoked to justify their actions.

It’s far from clear what the consequences of this increasingly aggressive Houthi campaign will be. The region seems poised for ongoing strife, and it’s an open question whether it will draw back in the likes of the U.S., which has been reluctant to return to full-scale regional conflict.

Yet none of that should obscure the plight of civilians in Yemen. Rather, it should serve as a reminder of the suffering of a population exhausted by a war that has lasted for more than a decade and has devastated the already meager infrastructure of what was the poorest country in the Middle East even before the conflict started.

Laurent Bonnefoy does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organization that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.

articles.title: Maricarmen Abascal: how a disabled, evicted 87-year-old woman became a political football in Spain’s upcoming election
articles.author: Dolors Palau-Sampio, Full Professor of Journalism, Universitat de València
paras: In Spain, an average of 44 evictions are carried out every day. While statistics like this are shocking, numbers alone rarely spark a revolution. Mass protest movements instead tend to rally around one compelling individual story.

This was exactly what happened with 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal, who has become so famous that she is known in Spain as simply Maricarmen. Following an insurmountable rent hike and a lengthy legal battle, she was evicted from her Madrid home of 71 years in September, and died on October 7. She quickly become a household name, and the figurehead of Spain’s housing protests.

Her case stirred the empathy of millions, and inspired collective shame that society was unable to prevent an elderly woman from being forced out of her home on a stretcher. Her story made headlines around the world, sparked a wave of fierce, nationwide protests, and led to an unravelling of Spanish politics that has culminated in a snap election on November 29 and a general strike planned for November 11.
Leer más: Spain’s snap election: will Pedro Sánchez’s latest gamble pay off?

But polarisation in Spain runs deep. While one section of society has embraced Maricarmen as a figurehead, another sees her as a target, a threat to be confronted. As the EU-funded PLEDGE project argues, emotions signal underlying grievances, and can either strengthen democracy or undermine it.

Political parties, partisan journalists and some mainstream media outlets – from the supposedly moderate or liberal right to the far right – have turned public debate on the right to housing into a hotbed of hostility. Maricarmen, the symbol of this struggle, has become an object of ridicule for conservative media and politicians.

Just hours after her eviction, Spanish newspaper OK Diario ran an editorial headlined with the stage name of a ventriloquist who shares her name, and who used to perform with a puppet representing an elderly woman.

It was a heavy-handed suggestion: Maricarmen was a puppet of the left, and was being used to divert attention from the government’s handling of the migrant crisis in Ceuta. Similar narratives have since been repeated in dozens of articles and television debates, in an attempt to discredit the woman who inspired the protests and, by extension, undermine the movement itself.

Shortly before Spanish right wing rejected decrees intended to ease the housing crisis, several media outlets set about dissecting the life of a pensioner who had become a household name just a few days previously.

Right-wing outlet ABC interviewed Maricarmen’s former landlord, in which he criticised her for living on subsidised rent. Meanwhile, El Español devoted a feature to a string of unrelated attacks on her character.

By the final days of her life, these conjectures had become widespread. Some outlets passed outright judgement: one outlet proclaimed that “The vulture is Mari Carmen”, a reference to the “vulture” investment fund that hiked her rent by 230% (complete with a misspelling of her name in the headline).

Sections of the Spanish press have even cast themselves as the ones setting the record straight. One headline published shortly after her eviction flatly stated that “Maricarmen is a chancer (and someone had to say it)”.
Polarisation makes it easy for attacks to spill over from Maricarmen herself to the protests and encampments in solidarity with her. Much of this hostility plays on assumptions and prejudice.

Outlets such as OK Diario portray the encampment in Madrid’s Puerta del Sol as an unsanitary space run by left-wing radicals in the service of squatting and indoctrination. La Razón points to the presence of knives, paving stones and vandalism at the encampment, warns of a possible scabies outbreak, and plays on classist prejudices about bad smells to stigmatise progressive organisations and their supporters.
Leer más: Spain’s housing crisis is a warning for all of Europe – rights mean nothing if they’re not enforced
The Objective, meanwhile, has scrutinised the wealth of people at the encampment. La Razón has run similar pieces that cast the movement as frivolous champagne socialists as putting on a show.
Madrid’s regional president, Isabel Díaz Ayuso, has also weighed in, calling the protesters “terrorists”.

On October 12, hundreds of far-right protesters – some waving Francoist flags and making fascist salutes – attempted to enter the camp in Madrid’s central Puerta del Sol square, and had to be held back by riot police.
Leer más: The antifa terrorism threat the Trump administration describes does not exist
With housing set to dominate the coming elections, political parties on all sides are doing everything they can to capitalise on Maricarmen’s legacy.

The left arguably has the upper hand on this front, and is making use of it – the emergency housing decree that the right voted down in late September was informally dubbed “the Maricarmen Decree”. However, some sections of the right are also trying to claim her as their own.

Just hours before Maricarmen’s death, far-right party Vox used her name to raise the spectre of immigrants enjoying privileges denied to Spaniards, with a post on X stating “If Maricarmen had been ‘Morocarmen’, she would have got social housing”. “Moro” is a derogatory Spanish term for North Africans.
Vox MEP Hermann Tertsch has even called for an autopsy on Maricarmen, fuelling a conspiracy that the government had her killed to help their campaign gain momentum.

People’s Party (PP) leader Alberto Núñez Feijóo, currently the favourite to win the November election, has struck a more sober tone but has still accused Sánchez of trying to “manipulate the emotions of the Spanish people”.

With seven weeks until the election, encampments continue across the country, and there is broad union backing for a general strike over housing on November 11. However, the same right-wing outlets that ridiculed Maricarmen now accuse progressive forces of exploiting her death, branding their campaign obscene, manipulative and necropolitical.

One thing is clear though. The political and media battle surrounding Maricarmen has conveniently eclipsed the core issue that led Pedro Sánchez to call a snap election in the first place: the state of Spain’s deeply broken housing system, and how to fix it.

articles.title: From ‘A Little Princess’ to ‘Black Panther,’ how Hollywood films have reimagined the South Asian epic ‘Ramayana’
articles.author: Sohini Sarah Pillai, Assistant Professor of Religion, Kalamazoo College
paras: American audiences will be able to watch an English-dubbed version of “Ramayana,” a Hindi film based on a South Asian epic tradition, in theaters in November 2026.

The Sanskrit “Ramayana,” or “Journey of Rama,” is an epic poem that was composed sometime between 400 B.C.E. and 400 C.E. The epic follows Rama, an exiled prince and an incarnation of the Hindu god Vishnu, as he journeys to rescue his wife, Sita, from the demon king Ravana.

For hundreds of years, people from different religious traditions across South Asia have retold the “Ramayana” through dramas, narrative poems, shadow puppet plays, pageants, folk songs, comics, television shows and many other mediums. Director Nitesh Tiwari’s upcoming “Ramayana” film is the latest retelling of this epic tradition.

For over a decade, I have studied how South Asian epics have been retold within and outside the Indian subcontinent. While many American moviegoers may not recognize the word “Ramayana,” they may have already encountered its characters and stories on the big screen.
Sita’s struggles in ‘A Little Princess’

A striking example is Academy Award-winning director Alfonso Cuarón’s 1995 film, “A Little Princess.” Although an adaption of Frances Hodgson Burnett’s well-known 1905 children’s novel of the same name, Cuarón’s movie begins with Sara Crewe – the daughter of a wealthy British Army captain posted in colonial India – telling the story of the Ramayana.

As Sara narrates the tale of Rama, the film presents scenes inspired by the epic. Actors portraying Rama and Sita are shown living in exile in a lush green forest. When Sita begs Rama to follow a demon disguised as a beautiful golden deer, Rama draws a magical protective circle around the princess and instructs her to stay within the circle’s borders. The story reaches a turning point with the demon king Ravana’s abduction of Sita after she exits the circle.

But the Ramayana is more than a story to Sara – it has parallels with her own life, especially after she is separated from her father when she moves to New York to attend boarding school. Cinema and media studies scholar Jyotsna Kapur explains that “the man cast as Rama is Sara’s father and the Ramayana is the imaginative thread that binds father and daughter together through their struggles while apart.”

At boarding school, Sara initially lives like a princess – like Sita – thanks to her father’s immense fortune. Yet after the apparent death of Captain Crewe in World War I, Sara’s headmistress confines the now-penniless child in the school’s attic.

While mourning her father, the heartbroken Sara uses a piece of chalk to draw a circle on the floor of the attic resembling the one Rama creates to protect Sita. Like Sita, Sara is eventually rescued – by Captain Crewe, who survives the war, and they return home to India.
By weaving these stories together, Cuarón used the epic’s themes of exile and separation to provide a fresh take on Hodgson Burnett’s classic novel.

The divine monkey Hanuman is one of the most beloved Ramayana characters. In the epic tradition, Hanuman is a loyal devotee of Rama, and he is the one who locates where Sita is being held captive in Ravana’s kingdom of Lanka.

Hanuman shows up in multiple different films. Pixar animator Sanjay Patel’s Academy Award-nominated 2015 short film, “Sanjay’s Super Team,” focuses on Sanjay, an Indian American boy who would rather watch cartoons than worship Hindu deities like Hanuman, Vishnu and the goddess Durga with his father.

Sanjay, however, gains a new appreciation for his family’s religious traditions when he reimagines Hanuman, Vishnu and Durga as superheroes resembling the three protagonists of his favorite animated television show, “Super Team.”

Ryan Coogler’s massively popular Marvel movies “Black Panther” and “Black Panther: Wakanda Forever” are set in the fictional African country of Wakanda. In both films, a character called M'Baku proclaims “Glory to Hanuman!” M'Baku is the leader of the Jabari tribe, a Wakandan community that worships a gigantic white gorilla deity.

In the original “Black Panther” comics, this gorilla god is known as Ghekre and is based on a deity of the same name revered by the Akan Baoule people of the Ivory Coast. But in the “Black Panther” movies, the Jabari’s gorilla god is referred to as Hanuman.

Hanuman is at the heart of Dev Patel’s 2024 critically acclaimed action-thriller “Monkey Man.” The unnamed hero of this movie is an Adivasi belonging to one of India’s many Indigenous groups. Hanuman inspires him to avenge the rape of his mother by a corrupt policeman working for a deceitful Hindu nationalist spiritual leader.

My current book project is about cinematic adaptations of the Ramayana and the Mahabharata, a South Asian epic tradition about a catastrophic war. I argue that “Monkey Man” draws from a variety of different narratives, including the Ramayana tradition and popular American revenge films like “John Wick” to shed light on key social justice issues in India, including sexual violence and Hindu nationalism.
Rama and Hindu nationalism in “Slumdog Millionaire”
Hindu nationalist interpretations of the Ramayana in modern India surface in the 2008 Oscar winner for Best Picture: Danny Boyle’s “Slumdog Millionaire.”
While many Hindus worship Rama, Sita and Hanuman as deities, Hindu nationalists have also presented Rama as a historical figure – the legendary ruler of the ancient kingdom of Ayodhya.

On Dec. 6, 1992, a mob of Hindu nationalists demolished the Babri Masjid – a 16th-century mosque in the city of Ayodhya in northern India. They claimed that the mosque had been built by first destroying a Hindu temple that marked the location of Rama’s birth. Following the Babri Masjid demolition, more than 2,000 people were murdered in riots across South Asia in 1992 and 1993.

“Slumdog Millionaire” follows Jamal Malik, an impoverished Muslim contestant on the Indian version of “Who Wants to Be a Millionaire?” When asked “In depictions of God Rama, he is famously holding what in his right hand?” Jamal has a flashback to the violent riots in the city of Mumbai after the destruction of the Babri Masjid.

As a 5-year-old, as Jamal flees the Hindu nationalist mob that had just killed his mother, he encounters a boy dressed as Rama holding a bow and arrow. The adult Jamal then states: “I wake up every morning wishing I didn’t know the answer to that question. If it weren’t for Rama and Allah, I’d still have a mother.”

The newest Ramayana movie’s tagline, “Our Truth, Our History,” seems to suggest that there is just one “accurate” and “historical” way to tell the Ramayana. This reflects a prominent Hindu nationalist ideology that the Sanskrit “Ramayana,” along with retellings that closely follow the ancient epic, are the only legitimate versions of Rama’s story.

Yet as indicated by Hollywood films like “A Little Princess,” “Slumdog Millionaire,” “Sanjay’s Super Team,” the “Black Panther” movies and “Monkey Man,” there is no single way to depict or understand this immensely diverse epic tradition.
