articles.title: After flood disasters, Nepal needs clear numbers on aid and a reconstruction plan
articles.author: Susmita Aryal
paras: Nepali communities live in the shadow of natural hazards, where uncertainty and fear are daily realities
Originally published on Global Voices
Settlements across the Tadi River, Devighat in Nuwakot District. Image via Susmita Aryal on October 7, 2026. Used with permission.

Forty-six days later, just when Nepal was trying to recover from the Bhotekoshi flash flood, which struck the Nepal–Tibet border regions, affecting Rasuwa and Nuwakot, another landslide-induced flood hit Chumnubri, Gorkha, on October 11, 2026. This latest disaster has added to the wounds of communities who live in the shadow of natural hazards, where uncertainty and fear are daily realities.

The climate-related disaster in Nuwakot has devastated a once-popular tourist landscape, destroying its natural beauty and economic opportunities, with settlements heartbreakingly reduced to rubble and vital infrastructure, including roads, bridges and hydro-power facilities, washed away. The full death toll remains officially unconfirmed.
Survivors still come to search for their belongings in Devighatm, Nuwakot District. Image via Susmita Aryal on October 7, 2026. Used with permission.

But an uncomfortable truth lies behind the devastation: The human cost of such disasters often goes ignored. Behind the statistics are stories of broken dreams, lost livelihoods, buried memories. There are families trying to stay alive without their loved ones, communities faced with an uncertain future, and countless people trying to make lives reconnect and rebuild from what little is left.

The task of rebuilding is huge. The damage is not only to homes, roads and bridges, but also to farms and local businesses. Kyodo News reports via AP that 7,500 homes were damaged or completely destroyed, with costs of recovery hitting USD 4.77 billion. The government has now moved from emergency relief to rehabilitation and reconstruction and has also acknowledged the risks posed by possible glacial outburst floods (GLOFs) and other hazards. The destruction of bridges and transport links has made surviving communities vulnerable and slowed reconstruction, exposing residents to further risk.
Buildings left standing, and homes left empty in the Bidur Municipality in Nuwakot District. Image via Susmita Aryal on October 7, 2026. Used with permission.

To this end, joint efforts are underway to rebuild damaged infrastructure and restore vital services. But pledged assistance is not the same as money that has actually been received and delivered to affected communities. Nepal’s Ministry of Finance’s foreign assistance tracker shows that Nepal has received USD 24.89 million in disaster relief funds. Such tracking can help bring transparency to the collection and distribution of aid. The Prime Minister's Office separately reported that USD 50.47 million of assistance (cash, materials, and teams) had been pledged.

No formal update has been given on the implementation of longer-term reconstruction plans. Most of the aid is still going to meet immediate needs like medical aid, food, and temporary shelters, such as tents.
What are houses without their people called? Photo featuring reporter Susmita Aryal. Photo from Bidur Municipality in Nuwakot District via Maya Devi Aryal on October 7, 2026. Used with permission.

Many affected communities remain far from rebuilt infrastructure and restored livelihoods. India, China, the United States, and the United Arab Emirates (UAE) are providing assistance, and the Asian Development Bank and other international financial institutions have committed funds. Yet recovery is likely to progress unevenly. The challenge for affected communities is not just to rebuild what was lost but to restore livelihoods, public services and a sense of security in the face of recurring environmental hazards.

In the following photo essay, Global Voices highlights how Nepali citizens are still affected by the disaster. All photos were taken by Susmita Aryal in Bidur Municipality, Nuwakot District on October 7, 2026.

articles.title: Poetry book promotes Chabacano, Asia’s only Spanish-based creole language
articles.author: Mong Palatino
paras: Ten authors and 23 poems are featured in the anthology
Originally published on Global Voices
Photo from the Facebook page of Voces del Alma. Used with permission

A new poetry anthology features writers of Chabacano, one of the Philippines’ 170 languages, which is widely spoken in the southernmost city of Zamboanga, and stands out as Asia’s only Spanish-based creole language.

The Philippines was a colony of Spain for more than three centuries, but the Spanish language was only used by the elite, friars, and colonial rulers. Only in Zamboanga did a Spanish-based creole language develop.

In 2018, Global Voices featured Bien Chabacano, a blog dedicated to promoting and documenting Chavacano de Zamboanga. Its creator, Jerome Herrera, launched a book project this year by inviting writers to submit poems to be compiled in an anthology. This led to the launch of the “Sombra y Luz” book in July, featuring 23 poems by 10 authors. The poems are mainly about love, family, and Zamboangueño identity.

Herrera said, “The project highlights not only the continued vitality of Chavacano as a literary language, but also the efforts of its speakers to create new literature and preserve the language through writing.”

He added that the book title aims to convey a message of contrast about the changes in Zamboanga City. The book cover also provides a nostalgic reference to the flowers that decorated the city in the past.

The cover features an American-era style lamppost that can be seen along the Zamboanga boulevard. The cover also features bougainvilleas which my dad tells me were ubiquitous in Zamboanga City back when it was known as the Ciudad de Flores.
One of the poems in the anthology, written by Jayline Gonzales-Barredo, mentions flowers and birds that enrich life in the city.

Maga pajaro que ta vola-vola, Na maga rama de pono ta queda, Alegre con uno y otro ta grita-grita, Twit! Twit! Twit! Entero el dia. Mio pueblo Ciudad de Zamboanga, Ciudad de Flores que llama. De noche mucho pajaro ay columbra, Na maga cable de corriente ta esta.

Birds that fly and flutter freely, Perched upon the branches of trees, Singing and calling each other joyfully, Tweet! Tweet! Tweet! All day long. Oh, my beloved City of Zamboanga, City of Flowers, they call you. At night, many birds can be found, Sitting on wires, that’s what they do.
In an interview with Global Voices, Herrera noted the heavy use of Spanish words in the selected poems:

…there is a lot of debate with regards to what Chabacano poetry should look like. For some, they like it with a lot of Spanish words and for others, they like it to be exactly as how Chabacano appears in everyday conversations. Most of the poems submitted leaned heavily on Spanish words, I think primarily because Chabacano writers rely on Spanish words to make their works sound more formal as well as more poetic. Since it’s poetry, I thought that it was alright to present Chabacano in an idealistic manner.
He added that the anthology seeks to encourage more people to accept the various ways that Chabacano is used.

For a very long time, people have been putting Chabacano inside a box. I hope that these books open up conversations regarding Chabacano literature and make people receptive to different kinds of writing styles in Chabacano.
This approach is evident in the poem “Escribi Chavacano, Conversa Chabacano,” which celebrates Chabacano as a living language.

Through references to poems, essays, fables, and the stories passed down by elders, the author reminds readers that the language continues to thrive when it is written, spoken, and shared with others. The title itself is noteworthy for its use of both Chavacano and Chabacano, reflecting the coexistence of two accepted spellings of the language. In doing so, the poem highlights not only the importance of preserving Chabacano, but also the richness and diversity of its written tradition.
View this post on Instagram
Herrera’s interview with Asymptote Journal noted the challenge of finding Chabacano contributors, and his hope that the book project can lead to more literary initiatives.

The biggest challenge is keeping the momentum going, since it’s hard to find Chavacano poets. Even so, I hope this anthology is just the beginning and that we’ll be able to publish a second volume in the future.

articles.title: How the ‘geopolitical stigma’ associated with Putin’s Russia is affecting ordinary Russians
articles.author: Marina Yusupova-Ryder, Visiting Lecturer in Sociology, Edinburgh Napier University
paras: Russia’s international standing collapsed within weeks of its full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Sanctions swept across Russian banks, businesses and political elites, while western companies exited the country en masse. For those living inside Russia, it was the everyday, tangible shifts that made this feel real.

Western goods disappeared from supermarket shelves, direct flights to Europe stopped and getting visas to travel abroad became more difficult. Russian athletes, artists and scholars, meanwhile, were excluded from international competitions, cultural platforms and academic events.

For Russians living elsewhere in Europe, the change was often more subtle. Questions about their nationality in job applications, negative media coverage and offhand comments about Russia all contributed to a growing sense that being Russian now meant carrying a stigma. Russia’s changing international reputation had suddenly become personal.

I have seen this transformation in my own research on Russian masculinities, which has involved interviewing Russian men living in Russia and abroad. When I first interviewed my 40 participants in 2013-14, most viewed Russia positively and had a relatively secure sense of national identity.
When I returned to interview 27 of them between 2022 and 2023, this picture had changed dramatically. Only two of the men still described Russia in unambiguously positive terms.
One of the questions I asked participants in the second round of interviews was: “How would you define Russia’s role in the world today?” Their answers were striking.

My respondents described Russia as “only a pawn in a big game”, “a bully with the nuclear baton” and “a pariah country like North Korea”. One participant even likened Russia to Voldemort, the main villain from the Harry Potter book series.

Two others called Russia a “backward, defective, sick country”, and “the state that uses violence to be loved”. Even those who supported Vladimir Putin’s regime and the war admitted that Russia’s standing in the world had deteriorated significantly since the full-scale invasion.

The intensity of the stigma – and, in some cases, the shame associated with being Russian – was palpable. Across the interviews, being Russian had become something that many felt they had to explain, defend, distance themselves from or rethink.
How my interviewees managed the geopolitical stigma was deeply entangled with ideas about masculinity, power and competition between world powers.

*Dmitry, a Russian man living in the UK, said: “I talk less about being Russian now.” He blamed the “incompetent” Russian authorities for the war and expressed sympathy for Ukrainians, yet still wanted Russia to win.

“Russia needs to win,” he said, because a victory would benefit Russian-speaking people around the world. “The victors are not judged – the winner writes history, as we know.” He feared that a Russian defeat would leave Russians as “outcasts” and argued that Russia should be able to “join the ranks of leading world powers like the US and Britain.”

Dmitry was distancing himself from the Russian state while simultaneously hoping that Russia’s status – and, with it, the status of Russians – would be restored through victory. His response drew on an idea of international power centred on strength, victory and the ability to command respect.

Petr, who was living in Russia, managed the stigma differently. “I’m not a political scientist or a military expert,” he said, adding: “I don’t have any plans for offensive military operations on my desk, I don’t know what’s really going on there. Maybe we’re victims of propaganda.” Disclaiming his agency helped him distance himself from the decisions of the Russian state.

But that distancing also became uncomfortable for his sense of himself as a man. He added: “I’m still a man. I am still a father, a defender of my family.” For Petr, masculinity offered a way to navigate this uncomfortable position. He could say he did not understand the war and was not responsible for it, while still claiming the identity of a man who protects his family.

Pavel, a respondent temporarily residing in a Mediterranean country at the time I interviewed him, took yet another route. He opposed the war and criticised Russia’s imperial violence. Pavel was particularly troubled by what he saw as Russia’s failure to acknowledge its past imperial crimes. He contrasted Russia with the “big guys” such as Germany and Japan, which he argued had already “repented” their imperial pasts.

Pavel was rejecting Russia’s imperialism. But he was also comparing Russia with other powerful states that he regarded as having become more modern and civilised. By positioning Russia as an empire that had failed to learn from its past, he could distance himself from the stigma of Russianness and align himself with a supposedly more legitimate international order.

As UK-based researchers Imogen Tyler and Tom Slater have argued in their work, stigma is not simply a label attached to those who are seen as deviant or discredited. It is a mechanism for producing and stabilising social hierarchies and unequal relations of power.

The men I interviewed did not simply accept the geopolitical stigma. They distanced themselves from it, challenged it or tried to overcome it. But in doing so, they often drew on the very ideas of power, victory, civilisational hierarchy and inevitability of violence that underpin imperial and masculine domination in the first place.
*The names of the interviewees have been changed to ensure their anonymity.

Marina Yusupova-Ryder received financial support from Edinburgh Napier University (ENU) to support the costs of conducting the empirical research discussed in this article. She is a Visiting Lecturer at ENU and holds a full-time research position at the University of Helsinki. Her research is currently supported by a grant from the Kone Foundation.

articles.title: What African elections can learn from the Borana Gadaa system
articles.author: Peace News
paras: Can the Borana Gadaa system inspire fairer elections, peaceful transitions, and stronger democracy across Africa?
Originally published on Global Voices

A Balli Walirafudhu handover ceremony held by the Borana Oromo people in Southern Ethiopia and northern Kenya. They have long practiced rotational, peaceful leadership transfer, known as the Borana Gadaa system. Photo used with permission.
This article by Diba Kosi Bilinga was originally published by Peace News Network on July 20, 2026. An edited version is being republished on Global Voices under a content partnership agreement.

Every election season, much of Africa braces itself. In some cases, incumbents amend constitutions to erase term limits, and citizens wait to see whether power will change hands at the ballot box or in the streets. The pattern repeats: disputed results, ethnic mobilization, coups, or leaders who refuse to leave.

Yet in the rangelands of southern Ethiopia and northern Kenya, the Borana Oromo people have long practiced rotational, peacefully transferred leadership. Known as the Borana Gadaa system, UNESCO inscribed it in 2016 as an Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity that regulates political and social life, resolves conflict, and protects women’s rights.

This article asks a question: What can African leaders, electoral commissions, political parties, and citizens learn from a governance model that has quietly rotated power every eight years for generations, without coups, without third-term referenda, and without the bloodshed that so often accompanies modern African elections?
Lesson 1: Power must have a time limit

Borana leadership rotates on a fixed eight-year cycle among five Gogeessas (parties). Each governs for one Gadaa period, then hands over power, returning to the first after 40 years — a rotation built into the structure itself.

Compare this to Africa’s modern pattern. Human Rights Watch (HRW) director Ida Sawyer describes a “constitutional coup” pattern: leaders who cannot win re-election simply rewrite the laws to get their way. Cameroon’s Paul Biya erased term limits in 2008 and has ruled since 1982; Uganda’s Museveni scrapped his in 2005; Rwanda, Burundi, Togo, Djibouti, and the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) have each amended their constitutions to extend a president’s tenure.
Gadaa’s lesson is structural: When a time limit is built into the system itself, rather than a leader’s promise, departure never has to be settled by force.
Lesson 2: Prepare leaders before giving them power

Gadaa systems treat leadership as something built over decades, not switched on by an election. Members pass through age-grades from childhood, absorbing law, custom, and ritual responsibility long before they are eligible to lead — knowledge oral historians formally transmit across generations.

Most African political systems do the opposite: Candidates are selected first, and asked whether they are fit to govern only afterward. Patronage, money, and ethnic arithmetic often outweigh demonstrated understanding of law or public finance, producing leaders who improvise governance while learning on the job.

The lesson for African parties and civic institutions: Build structured pipelines — in local councils, youth wings, and civil service — that expose future leaders to responsibility long before a national mandate.
Lesson 3: Peaceful transitions are a sign of institutional strength, not weakness

Under the Gadaa system, at the Balli Walirafudhu handover ceremony, authority passes from the outgoing ruling class to the incoming one, understood by the whole community as final and binding. Every eight years, the Gumi Gaayo assembly, held under the sacred Odaa tree, reviews the era’s laws and blesses the incoming leadership.

Contrast that with Kenya’s 2007 to 08 crisis, when a disputed result triggered ethnic violence that killed roughly 1,000 people and displaced 500,000, per HRW’s investigation. Ivory Coast saw a similar rupture in 2010 to 2011, leading to a civil war.
In the Borana Gadaa system, succession is scripted years in advance. In much of Africa, it is an open question resolved only after votes are contested.
Lesson 4: No clan or ethnicity should own the political system

The Borana society has two broad blocks, the Sabboo Sadeen clan and the Goonaa Bal’aa clan, each with its own sub-clans. But the five Gogeessa that hold political authority cut across these clan lines — political identity and clan identity stay separate, so no single clan can capture the system.

This fault line has broken many African elections. The violence in Kenya in 2007 to 2008 was driven largely by ethnic mobilization, with the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) noting ethnicity as the main axis political elites mobilize around — turning elections into an ethnic census.

Where political identity is inseparable from ethnicity, losing an election can feel like losing everything for a whole community. Gadaa’s design offers a template: build structures — party membership, constituencies, civil-service recruitment — that mix identities rather than reinforce them.
Lesson 5: Democracy is more than voting day

Gadaa’s Gumi Gaayo assembly does far more than confirm who leads. It reviews the era’s laws, arbitrates disputes, and holds outgoing leaders publicly accountable — through consultation among elders and councils of advisors (Hayyuu), not a ballot cast once every few years.

Much of Africa’s politics concentrates almost all democratic energy into a single day. ITUC-Africa cataloged disputed results across Guinea, Togo, Sudan, Burundi, Burkina Faso, Egypt, Comoros, Tanzania, and Rwanda in 2010 alone — accountability between elections proved far weaker than the contest itself.
Robust democracies need standing institutions — independent courts, electoral commissions, a free press and community dispute-resolution bodies — that keep working every day of the cycle.
Lesson 6: Leadership should serve the institution, not the other way around

The Abbaa Gadaa — the topmost Borana Leader — never rules alone. He operates alongside the Hayyuu council of advisors, the Abbaa Seera responsible for law, and the ritual authority of the Qaalluu — a deliberately decentralized structure, as one account puts it, designed to stop any office from concentrating too much power.

Across Africa, the opposite dominates. A 2026 survey found rulers such as Cameroon’s Paul Biya (in power since 1982), Equatorial Guinea’s Teodoro Obiang Nguema Obiang (since 1979) and Congo’s Sassou Nguesso (since 1979) have systematically dismantled the checks meant to constrain them. In each case, the presidency grew larger than the constitution meant to contain it.
When power is distributed across councils, courts, and customary bodies, no single leader’s ambition can capture the whole state.
Lesson 7: Resolve conflict through dialogue before It becomes violence

Borana layers its conflict resolution: The Kora Gossa handles local clan disputes, the Gumi Gaayo settles national matters, and Boran Haraamu Koo’puu Rules — a form of social exclusion — is reserved for those who break the community’s deepest trust.

Modern West Africa shows what happens when such mediation is absent. Since 2020, the Sahel has seen a wave of takeovers — Mali, Guinea, Burkina Faso, Niger, Gabon — linked to deteriorating security and falling accountability in the years before each coup.

The lesson is not that customary courts should replace constitutions, but that no state can survive on election-day mechanisms alone — it needs everyday channels of mediation to build citizens’ trust.
Lesson 8: Culture, memory, and inclusion are part of governance

Borana Gadaa’s institutions are inseparable from Borana culture. The Odaa tree is both a meeting place and a living symbol of continuity across generations. Knowledge of the system’s history — including a documented line of more than 72 Abbaa Gadaa — is preserved and transmitted by oral historians.

Governance needs more than law and procedure — it needs cultural memory, shared symbols, and inclusive channels through which groups historically shut out of power, especially women, can still be heard.

African leaders don’t need to build Odaa trees or revive age-grade systems to learn from the Borana Gadaa. They need its underlying logic: time limits built into institutions, leaders prepared long before office, structures that cut across ethnic lines, power distributed across bodies, and dialogue running continuously rather than waiting for crisis.
